  • The API Reference covers the same tools from Python.
  • Evaluation describes the scorer behind fsm-llm-eval.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Covers FSM-LLM v0.13.0

This page explains what the library is made of, where it fits, and how one message travels through it. For a first run go to the Quick Start; for the parts in detail go to the FSM Design Guide and Architecture.

docs.title: Why FSM-LLM?
docs.text:
FSM-LLM splits the work three ways:

  • The LLM handles language: understanding the user, pulling out facts, writing replies.
  • The state machine handles flow: which state you are in and where you go next is a rule, not a mood. The LLM breaks a tie between two equal rules and nothing else.
  • The framework handles state: what has been collected, history, your own hooks, and saving and restoring sessions.

Use it when the conversation has steps: forms and intake, onboarding, support triage, tutoring flows, anything where "what must happen next" is a rule.

Do not use it for open-ended chat with no structure (a plain LLM call is simpler), or when you need a hosted, production-hardened agent platform. The project is young, and one subpackage is explicitly experimental (see Status).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Every user message goes through two LLM passes:

flowchart LR
    U[User message] --> P1[Pass 1: extract data]
    P1 --> C[Update context]
    C --> T{Transition rules}
    T -- one fits --> S[New state]
    T -- several tie --> L[LLM picks one] --> S
    T -- none fit --> K[Stay]
    S --> P2[Pass 2: reply from the final state]
    K --> P2
    P2 --> R[Reply]
  • The context is a dictionary of everything collected so far in one conversation.
  • Transition rules use JsonLogic, for example {">=": [{"var": "age"}, 18]}. If several transitions pass, the lowest priority number wins outright. The LLM is asked only when two or more tie at that lowest priority. If none pass, the conversation stays put.
  • Pass 2 runs after the transition, so the reply comes from the state the conversation is actually in. A state with empty response_instructions makes no LLM call, replies with "" and adds nothing to the history.

The subpackages sit on top of the core and never the other way round:

flowchart TD
    core[fsm_llm core: API, FSMManager, MessagePipeline]
    reasoning[fsm_llm.reasoning] --> core
    workflows[fsm_llm.workflows] --> core
    agents[fsm_llm.agents] --> core
    agents -- ReasoningReactAgent --> reasoning
    monitor[fsm_llm.monitor] --> core
    monitor -- launch, builder --> agents
    monitor -- demo workflows --> workflows
    eval[fsm_llm.eval] --> core
    synthesis[fsm_llm.synthesis] --> core
    synthesis --> agents
    synthesis --> eval
    testing[fsm_llm.testing] --> core
Subpackage What it adds Maturity fsm_llm.reasoning 9 reasoning strategies as stacked FSMs, validation, up to 3 retries Tested offline; live behavior depends on the model fsm_llm.workflows Async in-memory workflow engine, 11 step types, a Python DSL Runs without an LLM unless you add LLM steps fsm_llm.agents 18 agent patterns, tools, human approval, memory, MCP, A2A, meta-builder Documented known limits in the agents README; open work is in the 2026 roadmap fsm_llm.monitor FastAPI dashboard, optional OpenTelemetry export Needs the monitor extra fsm_llm.eval Examples scorer (0 to 4), conversation cases with Wilson intervals Scores are a heuristic that overstates quality; read the logs too fsm_llm.synthesis A model compiles a goal into an FSM, gates judge it, a library stores it, a runner executes it; agent tools Tested offline with scripted models. Bench status: three blocks run on one model, all INCONCLUSIVE; no result favours synthesis. fsm_llm.testing Public test doubles, a scripted user and assertions for code built on fsm_llm (the fake LLMInterface doubles MockLLM2Interface, PromptGroundedLLM and ScriptedLLM, the reply builders, hash_embed, ScriptedUser with ConversationRun, and the assertions assert_state, assert_context, assert_path, assert_result with the opt-in PathRecorder) Offline; imports core only, never pytest

Evaluation honesty. The examples scorer reads each run's output with simple rules and gives 0 to 4. It overstates quality, and runs from before and after the 2026-09-29 restructure are not comparable. The method and the run log are on the Evaluate page. Offline tests (the default) replace the model with a fake, so they say nothing about model quality.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text: The library is organized into five pillars.

docs.title: The core: finite state machines driven by an LLM
docs.text:
• Two-pass turns: every message goes through Pass 1 (extract data) and Pass 2 (write the reply from the state you ended up in). Transition rules are JsonLogic evaluated in plain Python, so they are predictable and unit-testable. The LLM is asked to choose only when two rules tie at the lowest priority.
  • Handlers: your functions run at 8 points (start, before and after processing, before and after a transition, context update, end, error), built with create_handler. See Handler Development.
  • Intent classification: classification_extractions on a state, plus Classifier, HierarchicalClassifier and IntentRouter.
  • FSM stacking: hand a conversation to a sub-FSM and come back with its results (push_fsm / pop_fsm).
  • Streaming: converse_stream() yields reply tokens as they arrive.
  • Steps without a user message: advance() runs one turn and returns an AdvanceResult; run_until_terminal() repeats it within a step and time budget and raises RunBudgetExceededError when the budget is spent. Agents and the reasoning engine run on these loops.
  • Tool calling and structured output: a state with the optional completion field makes one native tool-calling or JSON-schema call. Core runs no tool; your handlers do.
  • Sessions and memory: save_session / restore_session with FileSessionStore, and WorkingMemory buffers.
  • Diagrams: build_fsm_graph(), to_mermaid(), to_dot() and the fsm-llm-visualize command.

docs.title: Reasoning, workflows and agents
docs.text:
• fsm_llm.reasoning: a solver that picks one of 9 reasoning strategies, runs it as stacked FSMs inside one message-free core run, validates the answer and retries up to 3 times. ReasoningEngine.solve_problem(problem) returns the solution and a trace.
  • fsm_llm.workflows: an async in-memory engine with 11 step types and a Python DSL (create_workflow, auto_step, condition_step). It runs without an LLM unless you add LLM steps.
  • fsm_llm.agents: 18 agent patterns (react, rewoo, reflexion, plan_execute, prompt_chain, self_consistency, debate, orchestrator, adapt, evaluator_optimizer, maker_checker, reasoning_react, parallel_react, verified_react, auto_memory, native_fc, swarm, meta_builder) plus AgentGraph.
  • Tools done properly: the @tool decorator, annotations, enforced timeouts, MCP and A2A support, tools loaded from folders of Python files, and standard operating procedures.
  • Human approval as a security boundary: a gated tool runs only with a driver-only grant bound to that exact call, which a caller's initial context can never set.
  • A meta-builder that designs FSMs, workflows and agents by chat (fsm-llm-meta).
  • fsm_llm.synthesis: a host FSM names a goal in a synthesize state, a model writes a child FSM for it, static checks, a bounded simulation and an optional approval decide whether it may run, a file-backed library stores it and a runner pushes it as a child of the host conversation (FSMSynthesizer, ProcedureRunner, FSMLibrary, create_procedure_tools). verified means those checks passed over a model-written spec, not that the procedure is correct. The tests are offline. Bench status: blocks s0, s1 and s2 are registered, run and recorded (one model, ollama_chat/bonsai-2:27b, for every role and arm, no strong/cheap split); all three verdicts are INCONCLUSIVE and no registered block shows a compiled procedure beating a ReAct agent. See Runtime FSM synthesis.

docs.title: Knowledge bundles and Agent Skills
docs.text:
• Open Knowledge Format (OKF): fsm_llm.okf reads, searches, validates and writes OKF bundles (a directory of markdown files with YAML frontmatter). fsm_llm.engine.okf_bridge.create_okf_handler() puts capped concept summaries into a plain FSM's context. fsm_llm.agents adds read-only OKF tools, a read-only memory backend and bundle exporters. fsm-llm-okf runs it from the shell. This follows OKF v0.2 (SPEC.md at commit ad30107, pre-1.0 and mutable).
  • Agent Skills: fsm_llm.skills reads folders with a SKILL.md from the paths you name (the open standard at agentskills.io as read on 2026-10-23, unversioned and mutable). fsm_llm.agents.create_skill_tools gives an agent three read-only tools (skill_list, skill_load, skill_read), and fsm-llm-skills validates, lists and shows them.
  • Untrusted by design: bundle and skill text reaches a model only as capped, control-stripped tool output (or labelled summaries), never as a tool description, instruction or persona. Nothing in a bundle or skill folder is executed, and allowed-tools is reported, not enforced.

docs.title: Monitoring and evaluation
docs.text:
• fsm_llm.monitor: a FastAPI dashboard (REST, WebSocket, vanilla-JS single-page app) to launch, watch and chat with FSMs, agents and workflows, with optional OpenTelemetry export.
  • fsm_llm.eval: scores the examples 0 to 4, or runs scripted conversations N times and reports pass rates with Wilson confidence intervals (EvalConfig, run_examples, run_cases, run_dataset, wilson_ci).
  • Pre-registered benches: scripts/agents_bench.py, scripts/skills_bench.py and scripts/synthesis_bench.py record blocks that are run once at a fixed n and never edited, so a number in the repository can be recounted from its rows.

docs.title: One LLM layer, security and reliability
docs.text:
• One LLM layer: litellm is imported in exactly one module, src/fsm_llm/llm/providers/litellm.py. LLMInterface.complete(CompletionRequest) is the single primitive for tool calling, plain and structured completion, with per-interface call and token counters (usage()) and an embedder (LiteLLMEmbedder). Any litellm model string works.
  • Cut-off replies are visible: a reply that stops at max_tokens is flagged (truncated, a WARNING, a named cause in extraction errors) and never shown as an unreadable half envelope.
  • Context security: internal keys (prefixes _, system_, internal_, __) and secret-looking entries are kept out of prompts. The compromised litellm 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 are below the required version, and make audit scans for malicious .pth files.
  • Assured reliability: an offline-by-default suite (a fake model, no network) covering the core, every subpackage, packaging, regressions, and the examples.
  • Decisions are recorded: # DECISION plan-<id>/D-NNN comments in the code say what not to do and why, and a gate (make decision-check) fails when one has no line in the manifest plans/ANCHORS.md. See Contributing.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
• Version 0.13.0. Most tests are offline and use a fake model, so they check logic and wiring, not model quality.
  • Evaluation scores are a heuristic and overstate quality. The recorded runs on the Evaluate page used a 4B local model, and scores on other models differ.

Things to know:

  • The fsm-llm command needs LLM_MODEL. The Python API takes model=, then LLM_MODEL, and raises ModelNotConfiguredError when neither is set (there is no built-in default model). Importing fsm_llm loads no .env file; read one on purpose with fsm_llm.load_env() or the --env-file PATH flag of a CLI.
  • The library logs nothing until you call setup_logging() or enable_debug_logging(); both also replace loguru's default handler, so a library record prints once.
  • One conversation handles one message at a time: a second converse on a conversation that is mid-turn raises FSMError.
  • constraints.txt pins every direct dependency and the dev tools to exact versions so CI and local runs match.

docs.title: Acknowledgments
docs.text: FSM-LLM stands on open-source work: litellm for the provider layer, Pydantic for the models, loguru for logging, JsonLogic for transition rules, and Ollama for the local models the evaluation runs used. Thanks to everyone who has reported issues and run the examples against other models.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The agent patterns, reasoning strategies and standards in this library follow published work and open specifications. Each pattern's module documents how it differs from the original.

docs.title: Agent patterns and reasoning
docs.text:
• ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models: Yao, S., et al. (2022). ICLR 2023.
  • ReWOO: Decoupling Reasoning from Observations for Efficient Augmented Language Models: Xu, B., et al. (2023).
  • Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning: Shinn, N., et al. (2023). NeurIPS.
  • Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models: Wang, L., et al. (2023). ACL.
  • Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models: Wang, X., et al. (2022). ICLR 2023.
  • Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models: Wei, J., et al. (2022). NeurIPS.
  • Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate: Du, Y., et al. (2023).
  • Building Effective Agents (prompt chaining, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer): Anthropic (2024).

docs.title: Standards and specifications
docs.text:
• Model Context Protocol (MCP): the protocol behind the mcp extra.
  • Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol: the protocol behind the a2a extra.
  • Open Knowledge Format (OKF) v0.2: SPEC.md at commit ad30107, pre-1.0 and mutable.
  • Agent Skills (agentskills.io): the SKILL.md folder standard, read on 2026-10-23, unversioned and mutable.
  • JsonLogic: the rule format used for transition conditions.
  • OpenTelemetry: the telemetry format behind the otel extra.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: • Probable Inference, the Law of Succession, and Statistical Inference: Wilson, E. B. (1927). Journal of the American Statistical Association. The source of the Wilson confidence interval used by wilson_ci.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: The Quick Start runs a first conversation, the FSM Design Guide teaches the shape of a good machine, and the API Reference lists every public name.

docs.title: Contributing to FSM-LLM
docs.text: Contributions are welcome, from a typo fix to a new agent pattern. Report vulnerabilities as described in SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
Work inside the project virtualenv. Every command below assumes .venv/bin is on PATH (or call .venv/bin/python directly).

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
make install-dev    # pip install -c constraints.txt -e ".[dev,workflows,reasoning,agents,monitor,eval,synthesis,testing,otel,a2a]" + pre-commit install

Upgrading a clone from before the 2026-09-29 restructure (extensions moved under fsm_llm/): delete the old src/fsm_llm_<sub>/ directories by hand (make clean no longer removes them), then reinstall with pip install -e .. After the package moved back to src/fsm_llm/ (plan d454fd62, step 62), reinstall with pip install -e . again; the old editable install pointed at the flat src/. A leftover directory imports as a namespace package.

constraints.txt pins every direct dependency to one exact version, litellm to a verified-safe release (1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were compromised; pyproject.toml excludes them too). Run make audit after installing new packages; it scans site-packages for suspicious .pth files.

docs.title: Tests, lint and types
docs.text:
make install-dev    # editable install with every extra, plus pre-commit hooks
make test           # Run full test suite (18,030 tests)
make lint           # ruff check src/ tests/
make format         # ruff format src/ tests/
make type-check     # mypy on the fsm_llm package (src/fsm_llm/)
make lint-imports   # import contracts in .importlinter (the Section 5.2 layers, kernel, litellm, testing, pytest, entry modules, ...)
make audit          # scan site-packages for malicious .pth files
make counts         # fail when a test count written in a .md file differs from a collection
make build          # wheel and sdist
pytest tests/test_fsm_llm/            # one suite (core)
pytest -m "not slow"                  # skip the slow tests
  • The default suite mocks the LLM: it needs no network and no model. Live tests need a reachable Ollama and skip without one.
  • CI (.github/workflows/python-package.yml) runs a lint job once (ruff lint and format check, mypy, the .pth audit, the import contracts, the decision-anchor gate and the workflow linters actionlint and zizmor), a supply-chain job (pip-audit --skip-editable over the installed environment, plus a canary that must see pip-audit fail on tests/fixtures/canary-vulnerable-pins.txt: never install or "fix" that file), a dependency-review job on pull requests (actions/dependency-review-action, fails on a high advisory) and a test matrix of seven legs: Linux on Python 3.11 to 3.15, Windows on 3.11 and 3.15 (macOS is not tested in CI). Every leg runs the .pth audit and pytest without the slow, real_llm and integration markers; the Linux 3.12 leg also measures branch coverage and runs the ratchet (scripts/coverage_ratchet.py). The Windows legs run python -m commands in bash, never make. Check an edit to a workflow with uvx --from actionlint-py actionlint .github/workflows/*.yml and uvx --from zizmor zizmor --offline .github/workflows (the lint job runs both at the pins of constraints.txt); every uses: takes a 40-hex SHA with its release tag in a comment, in every workflow file; tests/test_fsm_llm_regression/test_ci_workflow.py pins the matrix.
  • Pre-commit runs ruff (lint with --fix, and format) and the file hygiene hooks on commit, and a quick pytest run on push.
  • A behaviour change needs a test that fails on the code before the change. Run it against the parent commit to confirm.
  • Test counts are written out as literals in AGENTS.md and in CONTRIBUTING.md (the make test line above; the README is the PyPI page and holds no count), and tests/test_packaging.py checks them against a fresh collection. When you add or remove tests, re-measure with pytest --collect-only -q | tail -1 (and per suite) and update every literal. Never guess or adjust a count by hand.
  • tests/test_fsm_llm/test_docs_snippets.py loads every fenced block that names "initial_state" in the first-touch docs. A full FSM snippet in the docs must be a valid FSM.
  • Naming for new code (ids, units, constants, enums, builders, exceptions, verbs) follows the Naming conventions section of AGENTS.md.
  • litellm is imported in exactly one module, src/fsm_llm/llm/providers/litellm.py. Do not add a second request builder or provider call elsewhere.
  • Internal-key and secret-key checks go through fsm_llm.constants.has_internal_prefix and is_forbidden_context_entry. Do not re-inline them.
  • Anything new that is configured with many settings gets a step-by-step builder that follows the convention in src/fsm_llm/AGENTS.md: setters only record, build() is the only validator.
  • Commit messages follow <type>(<scope>): <summary>.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
The repository is one distribution (llm-fsm, setuptools, src layout). The directory src/fsm_llm/ is the import package fsm_llm (found by packages.find in pyproject.toml), so src/fsm_llm/engine/api/conversation.py is fsm_llm.engine.api.conversation, and a subpackage is imported by name, for example from fsm_llm.agents import create_agent.

fsm_llm/
├── src/fsm_llm/      # THE LIBRARY (the import package)
│   ├── engine/api/, engine/fsm/,   # API, FSMManager, MessagePipeline (the 2-pass turn)
│   │   engine/turn/, engine/kinds/
│   ├── core/definitions/      # Pydantic FSM models and core exceptions (a package)
│   ├── core/transition_evaluator.py, core/expressions/   # JsonLogic evaluation, no LLM
│   ├── core/verify/, core/visualize/   # Validator, data-flow and liveness analysis; diagrams and graph export
│   ├── handlers/              # Handler system, HandlerBuilder, create_handler
│   ├── llm/                   # LLMInterface and LiteLLMInterface (llm/providers/litellm.py is the only litellm import), reply parsing
│   ├── context/               # Context cleaning, compaction, filtering and the prompt builders (context/layout/)
│   ├── engine/classification.py, session.py, builders.py   # Classifier, session store, API/FSMManager builders
│   ├── security/, constants.py, logging.py, memory.py, env.py   # Key filtering, path confinement, limits, logging, working memory, .env loader
│   ├── okf/, text.py                       # Open Knowledge Format, text helpers (okf_bridge is engine/okf_bridge.py)
│   ├── skills/                # Agent Skills (read-only), the fsm-llm-skills command
│   ├── tools/                 # Tool registry, tool models and the @tool decorator (re-exported by agents)
│   ├── policy/                # Approval policy and the human-in-the-loop manager (re-exported by agents)
│   ├── frontmatter.py, cli_support.py   # The one YAML frontmatter loader, the shared CLI skeleton
│   ├── runner.py, __main__.py           # The interactive fsm-llm command
│   ├── reasoning/             # 9 strategies as stacked FSMs
│   ├── workflows/             # Async workflow engine, 11 step types, DSL
│   ├── agents/                # 18 agent patterns, tools, HITL, MCP, A2A, meta-builder
│   ├── monitor/               # FastAPI dashboard, OTEL exporter
│   ├── eval/                  # Examples scorer, conversation cases
│   ├── synthesis/             # Runtime FSM synthesis: compile, gates, library, runner
│   └── testing/               # Public test doubles, scripted user, assertions
├── tests/                     # One folder per subpackage plus root-level files
├── examples/                  # 100 runnable examples in 8 categories (evaluation baselines)
├── docs/                      # The documentation pages of the site (mkdocs.yml builds them)
├── evaluation/                # Datasets and recorded eval runs
├── scripts/                   # Supply-chain audit, benches, doc-count check
├── images/                    # Logo and diagrams
├── .github/workflows/         # CI: 7-leg matrix (Python 3.11 to 3.15), docs, pin refresh, release
└── CHANGELOG.md, EVALUATE.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, SECURITY.md

docs.title: Examples are frozen
docs.text: Do not modify anything under examples/ unless a maintainer asks for it. The examples are the evaluation baselines for fsm-llm-eval examples, and every shipped FSM JSON must keep loading (tests/test_examples).

docs.title: Plans, decisions and findings
docs.text:
Non-trivial work is done as a plan: explore, write a plan, execute it one step per commit, then review. Each plan lives in its own directory, plans/plan-<YYYY-MM-DD>T<HHMMSS>-<8 hex>/, holding plan.md (goal, steps, success criteria), decisions.md (numbered entries D-001, D-002, ... with context, decision, trade-off and reasoning), findings.md (what exploration found, with evidence), progress.md and state.md.

plans/ is gitignored. The one committed file in it is plans/ANCHORS.md, an append-only manifest with one line per anchored decision (<plan-id>/D-NNN | date | one-line rationale), so an anchor in the code still resolves after its plan directory is deleted. Never edit, reorder or trim its lines.

A commit made for a plan step starts with the plan tag: [plan-YYYY-MM-DD-<8 hex>/iter-N/step-M] <type>(<scope>): <summary>.

docs.title: Decision anchors
docs.text:
Code whose reason is not obvious from reading it carries a decision anchor, a comment that links it to a decisions.md entry:

# DECISION plan-2026-09-22T080837-8b258a25/D-036
# _fsm_cache_lock is a LEAF lock: while holding it do NOT take `_lock`,
# a conv_lock, log, or call fsm_loader. See D-036.
  • Format: # DECISION <plan-id>/D-NNN, with the full plan directory name as the plan id. Older anchors use the legacy form plan_YYYY-MM-DD_<8 hex>. A bare D-NNN with no plan id is not allowed in new code.
  • Add one when the code takes an approach chosen after another one failed, when a simpler-looking alternative was rejected on purpose, when it works around a library or framework constraint, or when a reader would reasonably ask "why not just do X?".
  • The body says what NOT to do and why. A new anchor is at most 6 lines; the full reasoning belongs in decisions.md.
  • Every anchor needs a line in plans/ANCHORS.md, the append-only manifest (one line per decision: plan id, number, date, one-line rationale). The line is produced when the plan closes; never edit or reorder an existing line. plans/ANCHORS.md is the one tracked file under plans/, so a fresh clone has it. The owner commits the appended lines before the first push.
  • make decision-check (python scripts/decision_index.py --check) is the gate: it fails when an anchor has no manifest line (and is not [STALE]) and when an anchor has a bad prefix (not a plan id, or a bare D-NNN). It reads the committed plans/ANCHORS.md only and takes no argument. A default-suite test runs the same check, and so does the lint job of CI.
  • make decision-index writes a report of every anchor to build/decision-index.md (ignored by git, never committed): each decision with its manifest rationale and every place (path and enclosing definition, no line numbers), so it is the lookup path from a decision to its code on a machine that has no plan directory. python scripts/decision_index.py --report prints the counts.
  • Read the anchors near code before you change it, and do not undo what they forbid. If a rule no longer fits, record a new decision that supersedes it instead of deleting the anchor quietly.

Two markers can follow an anchor's id:

  • [STALE]: the plan directory that recorded the decision has been retired, so the full entry may be gone (its one-line summary is in plans/ANCHORS.md). The gate counts such an anchor as resolved by its tag (it is listed in the index under Retired). The rule itself may still bind. Read the anchor text and the code around it before changing anything.
  • [SUPERSEDED BY D-nnn] (or an inline [supersedes ...] note on the newer anchor): the rule was replaced. Follow the newer decision; the old text is kept only as history.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
CHANGELOG.md follows Keep a Changelog 1.1.0: a ## [Unreleased] section first, then ## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD releases, newest first; inside a section the ### headings are only Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security, each at most once, in that order; and [Unreleased]: .../compare/v<newest release>...HEAD sits with the reference links at the bottom. Releases already published stay as they were written.

A change that breaks a caller (a removed or renamed public name or path, a changed default, a new refusal) gets one bullet that starts its breaking part with the exact marker **BREAKING:** (not **Breaking:**, not prose). The bullet names the old form and the new one: the changelog is the migration record of a release, and no separate upgrade guide is published. A **BREAKING:** marker outside a list item (a table row, a paragraph) is refused, because only a bullet is read for the spelling.

python scripts/changelog_check.py check                   # the form and the spelling of every BREAKING marker
python scripts/changelog_check.py check --from 0.12.0     # widen the scope to older sections
python scripts/changelog_check.py extract 0.13.0          # the notes of one release (also v0.13.0 or Unreleased)
make changelog-check                                      # the same check as `check`

The checker (stdlib only, read-only) judges [Unreleased], plus the newest release while [Unreleased] is empty. It is enforced three ways: tests/test_packaging.py::TestTheRealChangelog runs it on the real file in every test run, the lint job of the CI workflow runs the same command, and the release workflow reads the release notes with extract. In the release body a repository-relative link docs/... is made absolute under the tag by extract --link-base (a GitHub release body does not resolve a relative link); the changelog holds no such link today, and if you add one write it relative, never as an absolute URL to main.

docs.title: Building the docs
docs.text:
The documentation site is built from docs/ and mkdocs.yml with mkdocs-material. Its tools are a dependency group, not an extra (they need Python 3.11 or newer and are for maintainers), pinned exactly in constraints.txt:

.venv/bin/pip install --group docs -c constraints.txt   # needs pip 25.1 or newer
make docs                                               # a strict build into site/ (ignored by git)
make docs-serve                                         # live reload at http://127.0.0.1:8000

A strict build fails on any warning: a page missing from the nav in mkdocs.yml, a broken link or anchor, an include-markdown target that does not exist. A new page under docs/ goes into the nav; AGENTS.md files are never published (exclude_docs). tests/test_fsm_llm/test_docs_site.py checks the same structure without mkdocs installed.

.github/workflows/refresh-pins.yml refreshes the litellm and mcp pins of constraints.txt once a week (Mondays 05:17 UTC) and on demand (Actions tab, "Refresh pins", Run workflow). scripts/refresh_pins.py picks, per package, the newest release that is stable, not yanked, at least 7 days old (the cooldown: litellm 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were malware for hours, and a bad release is usually yanked within days), whose Requires-Python admits every Python of the CI matrix, and that stays in the major of the current pin; it never downgrades and never crosses a major (a new major is a decision, not a refresh). When a pin moves, the test job installs it and runs the non-slow suite (the mcp stdio tests included), mypy, the .pth audit and pip-audit, and only if all pass does the propose job push a chore/refresh-pins-<date> branch and open a pull request whose body is the script's report (old and new pins, release dates, ages, the newer releases skipped and why). The two jobs are separate on purpose: test executes a brand-new third-party release, so it has the read-only token and no credentials, and hands over only an artifact (constraints.txt, pyproject.toml, the report, uploaded before anything is installed); propose holds the write token, installs nothing and runs no project code, and a guard step refuses anything but those three regular files and any change beyond the litellm and mcp pin and range lines. A pull request opened with the default GITHUB_TOKEN does not trigger the CI workflow, which is why the gate runs in the refresh workflow itself. Owner action, once: Settings, Actions, General, Workflow permissions: tick "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" (without it the last step fails with a permission error and no pull request appears; the branch is still pushed). When a pull request appears: read the table, skim the upstream release notes of the new version, merge it, and close an older refresh pull request it supersedes. A red test job means the new pin broke the suite or has a known vulnerability: propose does not run, nothing is pushed, the pin stays, and the log names the failing step. Scheduled workflows run only from the default branch and GitHub stops them after 60 days without repository activity (re-enable in the Actions tab). Try the script without touching the repository: python scripts/refresh_pins.py --dry-run (reads PyPI, prints the table and the diff, writes nothing; --json-dir DIR reads canned <package>.json files instead). The tests are tests/test_fsm_llm_regression/test_refresh_pins.py (the script, canned JSON, no network) and test_refresh_workflow.py (the workflow).

.github/workflows/docs.yml builds the site strictly on every pull request and every tag v*, and a tag deploys it with mike to the gh-pages branch after checking that the tag equals src/fsm_llm/__version__.py (docs/README.md, "Publishing the site", lists the owner steps). Its text is pinned by tests/test_fsm_llm_regression/test_docs_workflow.py; check a change to it with uvx --from actionlint-py actionlint .github/workflows/docs.yml. Every uses: in a workflow is a full 40-character commit SHA with the release tag in a trailing comment.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
A release is one pushed tag. .github/workflows/release.yml starts on a push of a tag v* and on nothing else (no manual dispatch, no pull request, no branch push), so only a pushed tag releases. It builds the sdist and the wheel once, checks them (twine check --strict, the tag against src/fsm_llm/__version__.py, a final release only, the section of the version in CHANGELOG.md through scripts/changelog_check.py extract), writes an SBOM (sbom.cdx.json, CycloneDX, from a fresh environment with the wheel installed with every extra), then publishes to PyPI by trusted publishing with PEP 740 attestations (no API token exists anywhere), and finally creates the GitHub release with the distributions, the SBOM and the notes. tests/test_fsm_llm_regression/test_release_workflow.py pins the workflow; the distribution is llm-fsm (the import package stays fsm_llm).

The version bump (what the release commit of 0.13.0 did; the next one repeats it): set version in pyproject.toml and __version__ in src/fsm_llm/__version__.py (the subpackage __version__.py files re-export it); the three literal pins of the version in tests/test_fsm_llm_monitor/test_app.py and tests/test_fsm_llm_regression/test_regression_cli_and_exports.py; the README badge; the > Covers FSM-LLM v<version> header of the current guides in docs/ (and the lines that say the same in docs/AGENTS.md, docs/README.md, docs/concepts.md, AGENTS.md, src/fsm_llm/AGENTS.md, src/fsm_llm/README.md); in CHANGELOG.md, ## [Unreleased] becomes ## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD under a fresh empty ## [Unreleased], with the reference links [Unreleased]: .../compare/vX.Y.Z...HEAD and [X.Y.Z]: .../compare/v<previous>...vX.Y.Z. The release section opens with a short **Highlights** block before its first ### heading (under 8,000 characters, links in the docs/... form): the release body on GitHub holds at most 125,000 characters, release.yml cuts a longer body at 120,000 and points at the full text, so the Highlights are the part that always survives. tests/test_fsm_llm_regression/test_release_version.py fails on any place that was missed and on a section without Highlights.

python scripts/changelog_check.py check                   # the release section is judged while [Unreleased] is empty
python scripts/changelog_check.py extract X.Y.Z --link-base https://github.com/NikolasMarkou/fsm_llm/blob/vX.Y.Z/ > /tmp/notes.md   # the body GitHub will show, before the cut; `head -40 /tmp/notes.md` is the Highlights

Owner steps, in this order (the commands need gh logged in as the owner). Steps 1 to 3 are done once, before the first push of a plan's work:

  1. Commit the anchor manifest first: git add plans/ANCHORS.md && git commit -m "docs: anchor manifest lines". It holds the appended lines that make decision-check (and the lint job) need, so a push before this commit is a red first run on purpose. Never edit an existing line of it.
  2. In any other clone or virtualenv, after the layout move of 0.13.0: pip uninstall fsm-llm, delete a leftover src/fsm_llm.egg-info, then pip install -e . once (console scripts and the distribution name moved; python scripts/audit_pth.py flags a stale code-bearing finder).
  3. On PyPI, confirm llm-fsm is in "Your projects" and add a Trusted Publisher with exactly these names: owner NikolasMarkou, repository fsm_llm, workflow release.yml, environment pypi. (A TestPyPI pending publisher with the same names is an optional dry run of the whole path before the real tag.)
  4. Create the GitHub environment pypi with a required reviewer (you, with two-factor authentication on) and restrict it to tags v*. Without the reviewer publish runs unattended on any pushed v* tag; without the tag restriction a branch can deploy to the environment. One PUT sets the reviewer and the restriction to custom policies, then one POST adds the tag pattern. The environments API takes reviewers as an array of objects, which gh api field flags cannot express (they document scalar arrays only), so the PUT body is JSON on standard input, with real JSON booleans: the booleans as -f fields would be sent as the strings "true" and "false" and the API refuses them (422); with -F they would be booleans, but the reviewer would still be missing. The type of the POST is a string, so -f is right there:
owner_id=$(gh api users/NikolasMarkou --jq .id)
body='{"prevent_self_review":false,"reviewers":[{"type":"User","id":'"$owner_id"'}],"deployment_branch_policy":{"protected_branches":false,"custom_branch_policies":true}}'
gh api -X PUT repos/NikolasMarkou/fsm_llm/environments/pypi --input - <<< "$body"
gh api -X POST repos/NikolasMarkou/fsm_llm/environments/pypi/deployment-branch-policies \
  -f name='v*' -f type=tag
gh api repos/NikolasMarkou/fsm_llm/environments/pypi --jq '{protection_rules, deployment_branch_policy}'

The last command is the check: protection_rules must hold a required_reviewers rule naming you and deployment_branch_policy must read {"custom_branch_policies":true,"protected_branches":false}; the tag pattern is listed by gh api repos/NikolasMarkou/fsm_llm/environments/pypi/deployment-branch-policies --jq '.branch_policies' (one entry, name v*, type tag). The same in the web UI: Settings, Environments, pypi: tick "Required reviewers" and add yourself, leave "Prevent self-review" off (you are the only maintainer: with it on, nobody could approve your own tag), then "Deployment branches and tags", "Selected branches and tags", "Add deployment branch or tag rule", type "Tag", pattern v*. Required reviewers need a public repository or a paid plan. The PUT creates the environment when it does not exist and replaces its whole protection configuration, so run it once, before the first tag.

  1. Settings, Actions, General: tick "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" (the weekly pin refresh opens its pull request with it). Once the matrix is green, Settings, Branches: protect main, require a pull request before merging, and require the seven test (<os>, Python <version>) checks of the CI workflow (and lint and supply-chain). The pull request rule is not a formality: the coverage ratchet's guard (the baseline in coverage-baseline.json may only rise) runs on pull requests only, so a direct push to main that lowers the baseline file would pass check against the lowered file. As the sole maintainer, set the required approvals to 0 (a pull request, no second reviewer).
  2. git push origin main and watch the first matrix of seven legs. The Windows legs had never run before the first push: a failure there is a finding to fix, not a reason to skip the leg. The coverage tolerance is meant to be tightened after three green runs.
  3. Release from a clean main whose CI is green and whose CHANGELOG.md date is the day of the tag (edit ## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD if the tag is cut on another day, commit, and run python scripts/changelog_check.py check again):
git tag -a v0.13.0 -m "v0.13.0"
git push origin v0.13.0
  1. Open the run in the Actions tab. build and sbom run first; publish then waits for the environment review: approve the deployment. github-release follows. Check the result: the PyPI page of llm-fsm shows the release with its attestations ("Provenance"), the GitHub release carries the wheel, the sdist, sbom.cdx.json and the notes (they open with the Highlights), and pip install llm-fsm==0.13.0 works in a fresh environment on Linux and Windows.
  2. After the first docs deploy (the tag also starts .github/workflows/docs.yml): Settings, Pages, source "Deploy from a branch", branch gh-pages, folder / (root); then, from a clone of main with the docs tools installed (pip install --group docs -c constraints.txt), run mike set-default --push latest. docs/README.md, "Publishing the site", has the detail.

If a run goes wrong after the tag:

  • github-release failed after publish succeeded (the files are on PyPI): use "Re-run failed jobs" only. It reuses the artifacts of the run. "Re-run all jobs" rebuilds, and PyPI refuses files it already has ("File already exists"), so the GitHub release would never be cut. A failure before publish is fixed by deleting the tag (below) and tagging again.
  • .github/workflows/docs.yml also starts on the tag and deploys the site on its own, whether or not the release publishes. If a publish is abandoned (the tag deleted or PyPI refused it), remove that version from the site with mike delete <version> --push from a clone with the docs tools installed (deleting a version deletes its aliases too, so latest goes with it), then give latest back to the previous release with mike alias --push --update-aliases <previous version> latest. The two workflows are not chained on purpose: a workflow_run chain cannot be tested without a real run, so this sentence is the guard.

A tag that fails a guard publishes nothing: delete it (git push origin :refs/tags/vX.Y.Z and git tag -d vX.Y.Z), fix the cause and tag again. A version that reached PyPI cannot be replaced: cut the next one (the files of a release are immutable there).

docs.title: Good places to help
docs.text:
All taken from recorded open items:

  • Agents (src/fsm_llm/agents/README.md and the 2026 roadmap, open items): AgentGraph has no failure routing, so a fallback branch cannot be built; Orchestrator subtasks dropped over max_workers do not affect success; a reply cut off by max_tokens is detected (finish_reason, a WARNING, a named cause in extraction errors, no unreadable half envelope shown as a reply) and a cut final reply (or answer field) of an agent run ends it with success=False and stop_reason="truncated" (REWOO stops on a cut plan), but a cut native_fc tool call, a SelfConsistencyAgent sample, a long meta-builder artifact, a streamed reply and a cut in an earlier turn are still not flagged; Swarm never hands off by itself; real human-in-the-loop for REWOO, PlanExecute, ParallelReact and native_fc; MCP v2 and A2A v1.0.
  • Core (CHANGELOG.md, 0.12.0, Known open): validating an FSMDefinition for the first time from several threads at once can race; the message-free classification_extractions path has offline coverage only; nothing was checked live on a non-Ollama provider.
  • Reasoning (CHANGELOG.md, Known open): cheaper typed per-key reasoning fields were tried and reverted after losing answers on a pre-registered probe, so a new attempt needs its own probe; a final_context passed back as initial_context still carries the previous problem's analysis.
  • Measurement: every live number here comes from one small local model. Runs on other models and providers are welcome, as new pre-registered blocks (see scripts/bench_data/README.md).

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository and create a feature branch.
  2. Make the change with tests (see above).
  3. Make sure make lint, make type-check and make test pass.
  4. Add an entry under Unreleased in CHANGELOG.md. Name every public removal, rename and deprecation.
  5. Open the pull request.

docs.title: FSM-LLM Evaluation Process
docs.text: This document defines the evaluation methodology for testing FSM-LLM examples against LLM backends. It provides a repeatable, model-agnostic process for measuring framework quality over time.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# Automated parallel evaluation (recommended when the server can serve requests in parallel)
fsm-llm-eval examples --model ollama_chat/bonsai-2:27b --workers 4

# One worker: use it when the server has ONE slot (for example OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1)
fsm-llm-eval examples --workers 1

# Only a specific category
fsm-llm-eval examples --category agents

# Filter by name
fsm-llm-eval examples --filter react

# List discovered examples without running
fsm-llm-eval examples --list

# Fail a CI job (exit 2) when the health score is below 80%
fsm-llm-eval examples --fail-under 80

# Scripted conversation evaluation of any FSM (see "Conversation evaluations")
fsm-llm-eval run evaluation/datasets/simple_greeting_cases.json --trials 3

fsm-llm-eval is installed with the package (fsm_llm.eval, extra eval); python -m fsm_llm.eval is the same program. These are the only entry points. Run examples from the repository root, or pass --examples-dir, since examples/ is resolved from the current directory. Two behaviours differ from the removed scripts/eval.py: an --output-dir that already holds files is refused (exit 1) instead of reused, and usage errors exit 1 instead of argparse's 2 (exit 2 now means below --fail-under).

Output goes to a new evaluation/<timestamp>_<hash>_<model>/ (_2, _3, ... appended if that name exists) containing: - scorecard.md -- human-readable results with scores, timing, and category breakdown - results.json -- machine-readable results for scripting and diff - logs/<category>/<name>.log -- full stdout+stderr per example

docs.title: What We Test
docs.text:
Every run.py under examples/ is an evaluation target. The suite auto-discovers examples:

find examples/ -name "run.py" | sort

The count will grow over time. The scoring system is ratio-based (percentages), so adding examples doesn't break historical comparisons.

IMPORTANT: Do NOT modify existing examples unless explicitly asked by the user. Examples serve as stable evaluation baselines.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text: Category Tests Focus basic/ Core FSM conversations Extraction, transitions, response quality intermediate/ Multi-state FSMs Complex transitions, context accumulation advanced/ Stacking, handlers, concurrency FSM stacking, handler hooks, context isolation classification/ Intent classification Classification accuracy, routing correctness agents/ Agent patterns Tool use, iteration control, agent composition reasoning/ Structured reasoning Reasoning engine, validation, FSM stacking workflows/ Workflow orchestration Step execution, context passing, async meta/ Meta-builder Artifact generation, interactive building

docs.title: Automated (recommended)
docs.text:
Use fsm-llm-eval examples to run all examples in parallel:

fsm-llm-eval examples [options]
Option Default Description --model $LLM_MODEL (none: exit 1) LLM model identifier --workers 4 Parallel workers, one example subprocess each. More workers only help when the model server runs requests in parallel. On a server with one slot (for example OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1) they queue behind each other, and the per-example timeout counts the wait, so examples time out that finish alone: use --workers 1, or raise the server's parallelism --timeout 120 Default timeout per example (seconds) --category all Filter by category (basic, agents, etc.) --filter all Substring match on example name --output-dir auto-generated Exact output directory; must be new or empty --examples-dir examples Examples tree to scan --python the running interpreter Interpreter for the example scripts --config none JSON file of settings (flags override it) --fail-under none Exit 2 when the health score is below this percentage --list -- List examples and exit (dry run)

The runner auto-discovers examples, classifies them as interactive or automated, pipes pre-configured stdin for interactive ones, applies per-category and per-example timeout overrides, and runs them in parallel on a thread pool, one subprocess per example.

Timeout overrides (built-in tables in fsm_llm/eval/constants.py): - basic/intermediate: 120s (default) - agents/workflows/advanced: 180s - reasoning: 300s - Known slow examples (e_commerce, reflexion, orchestrator, etc.): 240-360s. The 23 examples whose agents run on the default AgentConfig.timeout_seconds (300 s) are at 360 s (budget + 60 s), so the agent's own timeout (an Error: Agent timed out after 300.0 seconds line) always comes before a harness kill; tests/test_fsm_llm_eval/test_timeout_table.py scans examples/ and fails when a harness timeout ties or is below an example's own agent budget. - The timeout clock also runs while a request waits for a busy server, so too many workers for the server's slots show up as timeouts (score 1), not as slowness: see --workers above.

Stdin scripts (EXAMPLE_INPUTS in the same file) are checked against the examples by tests/test_fsm_llm_eval/test_example_inputs.py: an example that never reads stdin has none, the meta/build_* scripts end without quit (the builder reads to EOF and would take quit as a message), and agents/react_hitl_combined is sent a task that names the gated publish_report tool so its y answers a real approval prompt (a model that skips the gated tool still turns the y into a second task).

A per-example value wins over the category value, which wins over --timeout, so --timeout cannot shorten a tabled example. To change a tabled value, pass a config file, for example {"example_timeouts": {"agents/debate": 400}, "category_timeouts": {"agents": 240}}; table entries in the file are merged over the built-in ones. Settings precedence is built-in defaults < --config FILE < flags; unknown keys are an error.

Exit codes: 0 the run finished (also with a low score), 1 usage error, bad config (including a file that is not UTF-8 or not JSON), unwritable output, a missing examples directory, or no example matched, 2 only when --fail-under PCT is given and the health score is below it (compared exactly: 116/200 meets 58), 130 interrupted. Ctrl-C cancels the examples not yet started and still writes scorecard.md and results.json for the finished ones, marked interrupted ("interrupted": true). SIGTERM (what timeout(1) and service managers send) is read the same way as Ctrl-C, for examples and run: the partial report is written and the exit code is 130. For examples the running example subprocesses are terminated too (step 12.34), so the process exits right after the report; before that it stayed alive until they finished. Before that change a timeout-killed run left a directory holding logs/ only; examples now also creates logs/ before the first example starts, so an interrupt before any example finished leaves logs/, scorecard.md and results.json. The handler lives for the run only, and is not installed off the main thread or over an ignored SIGTERM.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
# Ensure the model is available
ollama list  # for Ollama models
# or set OPENAI_API_KEY for cloud models

Which model runs. The model is --model, then the process environment LLM_MODEL; with neither set the run exits 1 with ModelNotConfiguredError's message (there is no built-in default). Importing fsm_llm loads no .env file (fsm_llm.llm sets LITELLM_MODE=PRODUCTION around its import litellm), so only the process environment fills LLM_MODEL. The scorecard and results.json name the model that really ran, so read them.

docs.title: Manual (single example)
docs.text:
For debugging or manual scoring of individual examples:

Interactive examples (have input() calls): 

echo -e "input line 1\ninput line 2\n..." | LLM_MODEL=$LLM_MODEL .venv/bin/python examples/<category>/<name>/run.py 2>&1

Automated examples (run to completion): 

LLM_MODEL=$LLM_MODEL .venv/bin/python examples/<category>/<name>/run.py 2>&1

docs.title: What to Observe
docs.text:
For each example, evaluate these dimensions:

  1. Startup -- Does it initialize without errors?
  2. Core Function -- Does it perform its primary purpose?
  3. Transitions -- Do FSM state transitions fire correctly?
  4. Extraction -- Are context fields extracted from user input?
  5. Tool Use -- (agents only) Are tools called and do they execute?
  6. Completion -- Does it finish without crashing or infinite loops?
  7. Output Quality -- Is the LLM output coherent and on-topic?

docs.title: Conversation evaluations (fsm-llm-eval run)
docs.text:
The example scores above come from a heuristic over stdout. To test a specific FSM's behaviour, write a dataset of scripted conversations with expected outcomes and run it several times:

fsm-llm-eval run DATASET [--model M] [--trials N] [--temperature T] [--max-tokens N] [--workers N] [--output-dir D] [--config FILE] [--fail-under PCT] [--list]

A dataset is a JSON list of cases, a JSON object {"config": {...}, "cases": [...]}, or a .jsonl file with one case per line. Each case has an id, an fsm (path relative to the dataset file, or an inline definition), optional initial_context, the user turns, and expect with at least one of final_state, visited_states, context (exact values), context_keys (present and not null), responses_contain (case-insensitive substrings) and ended. A trial passes when every declared check holds and every turn was sent (an FSM that ends before the last turn fails unless the case declares ended); a trial that raises (model down, bad FSM) is a failed trial with the error recorded. The sample evaluation/datasets/simple_greeting_cases.json has three plumbing cases over examples/basic/simple_greeting (unconditional transitions: any model passes) and name_is_extracted over evaluation/datasets/name_capture_fsm.json, which passes only when the model extracts the user's name. A useful case makes its pass depend on the model.

Each case runs trials times (default 3), in-process through fsm_llm.API, one fresh API per trial. Settings precedence: defaults < the dataset's config < --config FILE < flags, so a dataset that sets model beats $LLM_MODEL. LLM settings: temperature, max_tokens, and llm_kwargs (extra fsm_llm.API arguments such as api_base; recorded by key only). From Python, fsm_llm.eval.run_dataset(path, trials=5, checks=[...]) does the same in one call; a check is a function of the finished trial returning failure messages. The run directory (same naming as example runs) holds rows.jsonl (one row per trial, written as each finishes), results.json (per-case and overall k, n, rate and Wilson 95% wilson_ci, plus the config used) and summary.md. Report a pass rate with its interval: with 3 trials, 3/3 still has a Wilson lower bound of about 44%. --fail-under PCT compares the overall pass rate exactly (57/100 meets 57). Exit codes and Ctrl-C behaviour are the same as for examples.

docs.title: 3. Scoring Rubric
docs.text:
Each example receives a single score from 0-4:

Score Label Criteria 4 PASS Fully functional. All transitions fire, tools work, output is correct and coherent. No errors. 3 MOSTLY Works with minor issues. Core function succeeds but has cosmetic problems (wrong counter, extra loop iteration, slightly off output). 2 PARTIAL Partially functional. Some features work but key behaviors fail (transitions don't fire, tools not used, gets stuck). Requires workarounds. 1 BROKEN Starts but fails at core function. Crashes mid-run, hits iteration limits, produces wrong results, infinite loops. 0 CRASH Cannot start. Import errors, validation failures, crashes before any useful output.

Rules the automatic scorer applies on top of the table (since 2026-11-06, plan 0068b055): a run that exits 0 but prints a line starting with Error: (or Error during ...; indentation allowed, stdout only) or a line starting with Success: False is capped at 2 (failure codes F-CODE and F-MODEL), and an extraction rate of at most 50% (Extraction rate: 1/2 (50%)) is a partial failure (exactly 50% used to pass). Error: quoted mid-line in prose, Error Rate: metric lines, ValueError: ... and stderr are not read. Scores before this change (Runs 001 to 010) were given by the older rule, so they are not comparable with scores after it: an example that said it failed but exited cleanly could score 4. The heuristic still overstates.

docs.title: Distinguishing Scores
docs.text:
• 4 vs 3: Does everything work, or is there a minor glitch that doesn't affect the main outcome?
  • 3 vs 2: Does the example achieve its purpose (even if imperfectly), or does it fail at its primary goal?
  • 2 vs 1: Do some components work independently, or does the whole thing fall apart?
  • 1 vs 0: Does it at least start and produce some output, or does it crash immediately?

docs.title: 4. Failure Classification
docs.text:
When an example scores below 4, classify the failure:

Code Category Description F-CODE Code Bug Framework bug, not model-related. Fails with any model. F-MODEL Model Limitation Small model can't handle the task (bad classification, no tool use). F-TRANS Transition Failure FSM transitions don't fire despite correct context. F-EXTRACT Extraction Failure Pass 1 doesn't extract expected fields. F-TOOL Tool Failure Tool execution errors (calling convention, params). F-LOOP Loop/Budget Agent exceeds iteration limit or gets stuck in a loop. F-PARSE Parse Failure Can't parse LLM output (scores, JSON, structured data). F-SCHEMA Schema Error Pydantic validation, FSM definition errors.

An example can have multiple failure codes. Record all that apply.

docs.title: 5. Scorecard Format
docs.text:
After running all examples, record results in this format:

# Evaluation Scorecard
# Date: YYYY-MM-DD
# Model: <model identifier>
# Evaluator: <name>
# Example count: <N>

## Scores

| # | Example | Score | Failures | Notes |
|---|---------|-------|----------|-------|
| 1 | basic/simple_greeting | 4 | | Clean pass |
| 2 | basic/form_filling | 2 | F-TRANS, F-EXTRACT | Never reaches confirmation state |
| ... | ... | ... | ... | ... |

## Summary

- Total examples: N
- Score distribution: X at 4, Y at 3, Z at 2, W at 1, V at 0
- Overall score: <sum> / <max possible> = <percentage>%
- Category breakdown:
  - basic: X/Y (Z%)
  - intermediate: ...
  - advanced: ...
  - classification: ...
  - agents: ...
  - reasoning: ...
  - workflows: ...
  - meta: ...
- Top failure codes: F-TOOL (N), F-TRANS (N), F-MODEL (N), ...

docs.title: Overall Health Score
docs.text:
Health = (sum of all scores) / (4 * number of examples) * 100

A perfect run scores 100%. This is the primary metric for tracking progress.

docs.title: Category Health
docs.text: Same formula applied per-category. Identifies which subsystem needs the most work.

docs.title: Failure Distribution
docs.text: Count how many examples have each failure code. This drives prioritization: - High F-CODE count = framework bugs to fix (highest priority) - High F-MODEL count = model compatibility issues (tune prompts or set minimum model size) - High F-TOOL count = tool system bugs (single root cause, high leverage fix)

docs.title: Regression Detection
docs.text:
Compare current run's per-example scores against the previous run. Flag: - Regressions: Score decreased (something broke) - Improvements: Score increased (a fix worked) - New examples: First-time evaluation (no comparison)

Comparability break (2026-09-29 restructure). Since the extensions moved under fsm_llm, one library-wide logger.disable("fsm_llm") silences agents, reasoning, workflows, monitor and harness logs, and no example enables logging. Before, their warnings and tracebacks reached stderr, which fsm_llm.eval (scoring.py) scans for failure signals and which the per-example logs keep. Runs from before and after that change are not comparable, for agent examples especially: re-baseline before flagging a regression or improvement, and expect thinner per-example logs.

docs.title: 7. Model Compatibility Matrix
docs.text:
Track results across models to understand minimum viable model size:

| Example | qwen3.5:4b | qwen3.5:9b | gpt-4o-mini | Notes |
|---------|------------|------------|-------------|-------|
| basic/simple_greeting | 4 | 4 | 4 | Works on all |
| classification/intent_routing | 1 | 3 | 4 | Needs 9B+ for classification |
| ... | ... | ... | ... | ... |

docs.title: 8. Storing Results
docs.text: All evaluation results live in the evaluation/ directory. fsm-llm-eval generates output automatically.

docs.title: Output Structure
docs.text:
Each run creates a timestamped directory (the names below are an illustration of the layout, not directories that exist in the repository):

evaluation/
├── 2026-03-29_14-38_0aec60a_qwen3.5-4b/      # Auto-generated by fsm-llm-eval
│   ├── scorecard.md                            # Human-readable results
│   ├── results.json                            # Machine-readable results
│   └── logs/                                   # Per-example logs
│       ├── basic/
│       │   ├── basic_simple_greeting.log
│       │   └── basic_form_filling.log
│       ├── agents/
│       │   ├── agents_debate.log
│       │   └── ...
│       └── ...
├── 2026-03-28:10-15_36aed00_qwen3.5-4b.md     # Legacy manual runs
└── ...

docs.title: What Gets Generated
docs.text:
fsm-llm-eval examples produces three outputs per run:

  1. scorecard.md -- date, git commit, model, scores table (per-example with score/duration/failures), summary (health score, distribution, category breakdown, top failure codes), timing stats. "Total wall time" is the real elapsed time of the run; "Total example time" is the sum of the example durations (sequential equivalent). Scorecards written by scripts/eval.py before the fsm_llm.eval move labelled that sum "Total wall time", so compare old and new runs on "Total example time"
  2. results.json -- same data in machine-readable format for scripting, diffing, and trend analysis. The keys of the old format are unchanged; newer runs add wall_time_s, workers, default_timeout and evaluator
  3. logs/<category>/<name>.log -- full stdout+stderr capture per example, with metadata header (exit code, duration, timeout status). The example child runs with PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1, so the log of an example killed by its timeout holds the output it printed before the kill (earlier runs left such a log empty, which made a slow model look like a loop)

docs.title: Custom Output Directory
docs.text:
# Override the auto-generated path (must be new or empty)
fsm-llm-eval examples --output-dir evaluation/my_run

A run never overwrites another: when the auto-generated name already exists (two runs in the same minute on the same commit and model), _2, _3, ... is appended. Before the fsm_llm.eval move, such a rerun overwrote the first run's files.

docs.title: Comparing Runs
docs.text:
# Compare JSON results between runs
diff <(jq '.results[] | {name, score}' evaluation/run_a/results.json) \
     <(jq '.results[] | {name, score}' evaluation/run_b/results.json)

# Filter by model
ls evaluation/*bonsai*

# Check a specific example's log
cat evaluation/<run-dir>/logs/agents/agents_debate.log

docs.title: 9. Evaluation Log Index
docs.text: Quick reference for all evaluation runs. The raw run directories (scorecard.md, results.json, logs/) of Runs 001 to 009 were removed from evaluation/ on 2026-11-06 together with the other qwen3.5 run directories; the numbers in each entry below are the record. The scorecard text of Run 001, the last of these directories that git tracked, is recoverable from git history with git show 72388e6^:evaluation/2026-04-01_23-35_4025a78_qwen3.5-4b/scorecard.md (and results.json the same way). Entries that give a path name the directory the run wrote; it no longer exists.

docs.title: Run 001 -- 2026-04-01 (100 Examples, Honest Scoring Baseline, 75.0%)
docs.text:
• File: evaluation/2026-04-01_23-35_4025a78_qwen3.5-4b/scorecard.md (directory removed 2026-11-06; recover it with git show 72388e6^:evaluation/2026-04-01_23-35_4025a78_qwen3.5-4b/scorecard.md)
  • Model: ollama_chat/qwen3.5:4b
  • Commit: 4025a78
  • Examples: 100 (all with standardized verification output)
  • Health Score: 75.0% (300/400)
  • Score distribution: 63x4, 2x3, 7x2, 28x1, 0x0
  • Category breakdown: workflows 100% (8/8), classification 100% (4/4), reasoning 100% (1/1), agents 95.8% (46/48 pass), meta 80% (2 pass, 3 partial), basic 7% (1/14 pass — only multi_turn_extraction), advanced 12% (1/17 pass — only yoga_instructions), intermediate 44% (adaptive_quiz partial, book_recommendation partial, product_recommendation broken)
  • Top failure codes: F-EXTRACT (35), F-TRANS (28), F-LOOP (2), F-CODE (1)
  • Root cause: FSM field extraction on 4B model fails across most basic/intermediate/advanced examples. The 2-pass architecture's Pass 1 (data extraction) does not reliably extract named fields — the model generates good conversational responses but returns no structured extraction data. Agent, workflow, classification, and meta examples work because they use different execution patterns (tool calling, step execution, intent classification) that don't rely on FSM field extraction.
  • Note: This is the first honest baseline. All prior runs (001-012) used eval scoring that only checked exit codes, allowing examples with 0% extraction to score PASS. Those runs have been invalidated and removed.

docs.title: Run 002 -- 2026-04-02 (100 Examples, Extraction Pipeline Improvements, 88.0%)
docs.text:
• File: evaluation/2026-04-02_08-28_830692b_qwen3.5-4b/scorecard.md (directory removed 2026-11-06)
  • Model: ollama_chat/qwen3.5:4b
  • Commit: 830692b
  • Examples: 100
  • Health Score: 88.0% (352/400) -- +13.0pp from Run 001
  • Score distribution: 82x4, 0x3, 6x2, 12x1, 0x0
  • Category breakdown: advanced 96% (+84pp), basic 86% (+79pp), agents 86%, intermediate 67% (+23pp), classification 100%, workflows 100%, reasoning 100%, meta 70%
  • Top failure codes: F-EXTRACT (9), F-LOOP (9), F-TRANS (3)
  • Changes made (all in src/, no example modifications):
  • Simplified field extraction prompt: replaced verbose XML+CDATA with concise plain text optimized for 4B models
  • Post-transition extraction: after a state transition, re-extract in the new state from the same user message (skipped for agent FSMs)
  • Transition condition scanning: extract fields from transition requires_context_keys, not just state required_context_keys
  • Bulk extraction fallback: for states with extraction_instructions but no explicit field configs
  • Partial/relative value acceptance: prompts now accept "next Saturday" for dates, "around 7pm" for times
  • Date context: today's date included in extraction prompts
  • JSON parsing improvements: markdown fence stripping, extracted_data wrapper fallback
  • Conversation data cache: get_data()/get_current_state() work after end_conversation()
  • Remaining failures: Agent timeouts (9, model limitation), 2 basic examples without required_context_keys, 3 meta builder stdin issues
  • Note: This is the new official baseline. Agent score varies between runs due to non-deterministic LLM output (agent patterns are sensitive to exact model responses). The framework changes do not cause regressions — agent FSMs are explicitly excluded from post-transition extraction.

docs.title: Run 005 -- 2026-04-02 (100 Examples, Iterative Improvements, 95.8%)
docs.text:
• File: evaluation/2026-04-02_16-11_0b2b7f8_qwen3.5-4b/scorecard.md (directory removed 2026-11-06)
  • Model: ollama_chat/qwen3.5:4b
  • Commit: 0b2b7f8
  • Examples: 100
  • Health Score: 95.8% (383/400) -- +5.0pp from Run 004, +20.8pp from Run 001
  • Score distribution: 94x4, 0x3, 1x2, 5x1, 0x0
  • Category breakdown: advanced 97%, basic 100% (+4pp), agents 94% (+5pp), intermediate 100% (+25pp), classification 81%, workflows 100%, reasoning 100%, meta 100% (+30pp)
  • Top failure codes: F-LOOP (5), F-EXTRACT (1)
  • Changes made (all in src/ and scripts/, no example modifications):
  • Orchestrator/EvalOpt FSM deadlock fix: added fallback unconditional transitions (priority 900) to orchestrator collect and evaluator-optimizer evaluate states, preventing deadlock when LLM fails to extract transition-triggering fields
  • Type validation: FSMManager.start_conversation() now raises FSMError instead of AttributeError when initial_context is not a dict
  • Extraction prompt improvement: field extraction now explicitly guides LLMs to check conversation history when value is not in current message
  • Default extraction retries: changed from 0 to 1, giving each required field one retry pass
  • Structured output terminal-only: response_format (JSON schema enforcement) now only applied on terminal FSM states, preventing small models from hanging on intermediate states
  • Field name echo rejection: extraction validation now rejects values that match the field name (model confusion artifact)
