docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Covers FSM-LLM v0.13.0

The repository holds 100 runnable examples in 8 categories. Each is a folder with a run.py and its FSM JSON. The examples are not part of this site: the links below open the folders on GitHub.

The examples are not in the installed package (pip install llm-fsm). Clone the repository to get them (git clone https://github.com/NikolasMarkou/fsm_llm.git) and run one from the clone:

python examples/basic/simple_greeting/run.py     # needs a model: an OpenAI key, or a local Ollama

Set the model first (LLM_MODEL, see the Quick Start); an example makes real model calls.

Category Count Highlights Basic 14 simple_greeting, form_filling, multi_turn_extraction Intermediate 3 book_recommendation, product_recommendation, adaptive_quiz Advanced 17 e_commerce (FSM stacking), support_pipeline, concurrent_conversations Classification 4 intent_routing, smart_helpdesk, multi_intent Reasoning 1 math_tutor Workflows 8 order_processing, parallel_steps, conditional_branching Agents 48 react_search, plan_execute, reflexion, debate, orchestrator Meta 5 build_fsm, build_workflow, build_agent

All of them are on GitHub under examples/.

docs.title: They are evaluation baselines
docs.text: The examples are the baselines for fsm-llm-eval examples, which runs them in parallel and scores each from 0 to 4. The score is a heuristic that overstates quality; see Evaluate for the method and the recorded runs, and the command line page for the flags. Do not edit the examples unless a maintainer asks: changing one moves the baseline.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: The Quick Start builds a first conversation, and the Command line page lists the flags of fsm-llm-eval.

docs.title: FSM Design Guide
docs.text:
Covers FSM-LLM v0.13.0

Best practices for designing effective Finite State Machines for conversational AI.

docs.title: 1. Single Responsibility States
docs.text:
Each state should have one clear purpose:

{
  "collect_email": {
    "id": "collect_email",
    "description": "Collect the user's email address",
    "purpose": "Collect and validate user's email address",
    "extraction_instructions": "Extract the user's email address",
    "response_instructions": "Ask for email, or confirm the one provided",
    "required_context_keys": ["email"],
    "transitions": [{"target_state": "collect_phone", "description": "Valid email provided"}]
  }
}

Avoid states that try to collect everything at once.

docs.title: 2. Clear Transition Logic
docs.text:
Make conditions explicit with JsonLogic:

{
  "transitions": [
    {
      "target_state": "vip_service",
      "description": "High-value customer",
      "conditions": [{
        "description": "Lifetime value above 1000",
        "requires_context_keys": ["lifetime_value"],
        "logic": {">": [{"var": "lifetime_value"}, 1000]}
      }]
    },
    {"target_state": "standard_service", "description": "Default path"}
  ]
}

docs.title: 3. Graceful Error Handling
docs.text: Always provide paths for error cases -- avoid dead-end states with no transitions.

docs.title: 4. Natural Language Cues
docs.text:
Write purposes that guide natural conversation:

{
  "purpose": "Warmly greet the returning customer by name and ask how we can help",
  "response_instructions": "Use the customer's name and offer a personalized welcome",
  "required_context_keys": ["customer_name"]
}

docs.title: The Gatekeeper -- Authentication/Validation
docs.text:
{
  "verify_identity": {
    "purpose": "Verify user identity with security questions",
    "required_context_keys": ["account_number", "security_answer"],
    "transitions": [
      {"target_state": "authenticated", "description": "Identity verified"},
      {"target_state": "auth_failed", "description": "Failed verification"}
    ]
  }
}

With no conditions and equal (default) priorities, both transitions pass and tie, so they are ambiguous and the LLM picks between them from the descriptions. (Two tied transitions to the same target are one candidate and need no choice. A tie of 15 or more distinct targets cannot be classified: the conversation stays in the state and fsm-llm-validate warns.) Among passing transitions the unique lowest priority value wins outright, so to make "Identity verified" deterministic, give each transition a condition with requires_context_keys and a logic so only one passes, or give it a lower priority than the fallback edge.

docs.title: The Collector -- Gathering Information
docs.text:
{
  "shipping_address": {
    "purpose": "Collect complete shipping address",
    "extraction_instructions": "Extract street, city, state, and zip code",
    "required_context_keys": ["street", "city", "state", "zip"],
    "transitions": [{
      "target_state": "confirm_address",
      "description": "All fields collected",
      "conditions": [{
        "description": "Every address field is present",
        "requires_context_keys": ["street", "city", "state", "zip"],
        "logic": {"and": [
          {"has_context": "street"}, {"has_context": "city"},
          {"has_context": "state"}, {"has_context": "zip"}
        ]}
      }]
    }]
  }
}

The condition is what holds the state until the address is complete; required_context_keys alone only asks the pipeline to extract those keys.

docs.title: The Router -- Directing to Specialized Flows
docs.text:
{
  "issue_classifier": {
    "purpose": "Understand the issue type and route appropriately",
    "transitions": [
      {"target_state": "technical_flow", "description": "Technical issue"},
      {"target_state": "billing_flow", "description": "Billing issue"},
      {"target_state": "general_inquiry", "description": "General question"}
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: The Confirmer -- Validating Understanding
docs.text:
{
  "confirm_order": {
    "purpose": "Summarize order details and get final confirmation",
    "transitions": [
      {"target_state": "process_order", "description": "Confirmed"},
      {"target_state": "modify_order", "description": "Wants changes"}
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Transition Field Reference
docs.text:
evaluation_priority on TransitionCondition: Controls evaluation order (default 100, range 0-1000). Lower values evaluated first -- useful for short-circuiting:

{"conditions": [
  {"description": "Account suspended", "logic": {"==": [{"var": "account_status"}, "suspended"]}, "evaluation_priority": 10},
  {"description": "Account overdue", "logic": {"==": [{"var": "payment_status"}, "overdue"]}, "evaluation_priority": 50}
]}

llm_description on Transition: Optional string (max 300 chars) that customizes how a transition is presented to the LLM during ambiguous decisions. When omitted, description is used.

docs.title: Context Management
docs.text:
Required vs optional: required_context_keys lists the data a state should extract; it does not block a transition (an unconditional transition fires even when a listed key is missing). To hold a state until data exists, give the transition a condition with requires_context_keys and a logic such as {"has_context": "email"}; fsm-llm-validate warns about a required key no condition gates on.

Progressive building: Collect information gradually across states rather than all at once.

Context scope: context_scope.read_keys restricts which context keys a state's prompts see. write_keys is advisory: it is not enforced. Both must be lists of strings, and any other key in context_scope (for example a misspelt read_key) is a load error.

Gate keys the user must not set: a key a transition condition reads (is_admin, is_verified) can be written by a steered extraction unless you list it in the FSM-level handler_only_keys. Listed keys are dropped from every LLM extraction channel and stay writable by handlers, update_context and initial_context. It is opt-in and covers only the listed keys (an unlisted gate key, or one owned by a classification_extractions entry, is not protected). fsm-llm-validate warns about a listed key no state references (usually a typo) and about a listed key that a classification_extractions entry writes.

Corrections: a later-turn value the LLM returns for an already-set key replaces it only when the pipeline extracted that key itself (handler-set and update_context values are never overwritten). A refused correction leaves the stored value in place, and the Pass-2 prompt then carries a <rejected_corrections> block so the reply does not claim the change was made. The block appears only when the user's message states the value as a whole word of at least 3 characters (bored does not ground red; a 1 or 2 character value such as US never does), and never for a value that ended up stored. A handler that normalises an extracted value on CONTEXT_UPDATE (blue -> BLUE) counts as a handler edit and turns later corrections of that key off (the stored value stands and the reply is told so).

docs.title: FSM Stacking Patterns
docs.text: FSM stacking (push_fsm/pop_fsm) enables modular, composable design.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Shared sub-flows -- A "collect address" FSM reused by checkout, returns, account setup
  • Progressive detail -- High-level routing FSM pushes specialized FSMs per topic
  • Reasoning integration -- The reasoning engine uses stacking internally

docs.title: Guidelines
docs.text:
1. Keep child FSMs self-contained -- they should work independently
  2. Define clear context contracts via context_to_pass and shared_context_keys
  3. Design terminal states (no outgoing transitions) to trigger pop_fsm
  4. Choose merge strategies: "update" (overwrite parent) or "preserve" (only add new keys). Only keys named in shared_context_keys (or given as return_context / context_to_return) come back, whatever the strategy; a child's other extracted data is dropped on pop.
api.push_fsm(conv_id, "address_form.json",
    context_to_pass={"flow": "checkout"},
    shared_context_keys=["user_id"])

api.pop_fsm(conv_id,
    context_to_return={"address_complete": True},
    merge_strategy="update")

docs.title: Classification-Based Routing
docs.text:
Classification is built into the core (fsm_llm.Classifier). Use it with classification_extractions on states for automatic intent-based routing, or use a lightweight classifier layer that pushes the appropriate FSM via stacking.

Inside a conversation the classifier uses the conversation's own LLM interface, so a custom llm_interface given to API also answers the classification calls. An entry that sets its own model gets a separate interface for that model (no connection settings are copied to it).

docs.title: Tool Calling and Structured Turns (completion)
docs.text:
A state may declare the optional completion field. Its Pass 1 is then one native tool-calling call (tools) or one JSON-schema call (response_format_key, an internal context key holding the response format), never both, over [system(instructions)] + context[messages_key]. The result {kind, text, calls} lands in result_key (default completion_result), and transitions route on <result_key>.kind:

"transitions": [
  {"target_state": "run_tools", "description": "The model called tools", "priority": 10,
   "conditions": [{"description": "Calls", "logic": {"==": [{"var": "completion_result.kind"}, "calls"]}}]},
  {"target_state": "conclude", "description": "Final answer or malformed turn", "priority": 900}
]

Design rules:

  • Give every result kind (calls, final, malformed; no calls without tools) a route, or end on an unconditional fallback edge; fsm-llm-validate warns otherwise.
  • The transcript (messages_key, default _completion_messages) belongs to you: seed it with the task as a user message, and after running the calls append fsm_llm.tool_exchange(text, calls, results). Core refuses an unpaired transcript and a tool-calling turn with no user message.
  • The call runs only while result_key is unset: the handler that acts on a result clears it, otherwise the state makes no new call.
  • A completion state has no other extraction (field_extractions, classification_extractions, required_context_keys, extraction_instructions) and cannot be terminal. Leave its response_instructions empty unless it should also speak.
  • Core runs no tool. Run tools in a handler on the next state (the native_fc agent does exactly this).

docs.title: Procedures Written on Demand (synthesize)
docs.text:
A state may declare the optional synthesize field when a sub-conversation cannot be written ahead of time. The state carries a goal; fsm_llm.synthesis.ProcedureRunner has a model write a child FSM for it, checks it, runs it on the host's model as a pushed child and merges back only the declared return_keys. The state itself is silent and routes on the result the runner writes to synthesis_result:

"gather": {
  "id": "gather", "description": "Run a procedure written on demand", "purpose": "Collect the booking",
  "response_instructions": "",
  "synthesize": {"goal": "Book a table: ask the party size and the date.",
                 "inputs": ["venue"], "return_keys": ["party_size", "visit_date"], "on_failure": "sorry"},
  "transitions": [
    {"target_state": "done", "description": "It finished", "priority": 1,
     "conditions": [{"description": "ok", "requires_context_keys": ["synthesis_result"],
                     "logic": {"==": [{"var": "synthesis_result.status"}, "ok"]}}]},
    {"target_state": "sorry", "description": "It failed or was stopped", "priority": 2,
     "conditions": [{"description": "not ok", "requires_context_keys": ["synthesis_result"],
                     "logic": {"in": [{"var": "synthesis_result.status"}, ["failed", "aborted"]]}}]}
  ]
}

Design rules:

  • Route on synthesis_result.status (ok, failed, aborted; running while it works). Every edge must read the result key, or it would fire before the runner has produced a result.
  • Write the failure edge as status in [failed, aborted]. A procedure that spends its turn budget ends aborted, so a bare == "failed" would strand the host: the loader runs the edges on sample results and refuses it.
  • on_failure names the state the failure edge reaches, one of the state's own transition targets. Give that state a reply that apologises or offers an alternative, because a failure is a normal outcome, not an exception.
  • Name what the procedure may use (inputs) and what it must return (return_keys) with plain key names. Do not use a handler-only key as a return key.
  • The state declares no extraction and no completion. Core only loads the field: a bare API.converse stays in the state, so drive the host through ProcedureRunner.
  • The result is skip-if-set. A state that runs again on re-entry must clear synthesis_result first (clear_keys_on_entry).

The guide is synthesis.md; the reference is the Synthesis section of api_reference.md.

docs.title: Designing for Agents
docs.text:
Agent patterns (fsm_llm.agents) auto-generate FSMs from tool registries. The core ReAct loop is a 3-4 state FSM: Think -> Act -> Observe -> Conclude. Tool execution happens via handlers, not state instructions.

For agent-style flows that accumulate intermediate results across turns, WorkingMemory (fsm_llm.WorkingMemory) provides named buffers (core, scratch, environment, reasoning) so tool outputs and intermediate reasoning are organized rather than flattened into one context dict. Note the reach: buffer data is merged into the Pass-1 per-field extraction prompt only (default context_keys), never into the Pass-2 response prompt, which reads context.data alone; put anything the response model must see in context.data (via update_context or a handler). Intermediate states can also set an empty response_instructions to skip the Pass-2 response LLM call entirely (see the 2-pass notes), which is the common pattern for tool-dispatch states inside a ReAct loop.

docs.title: Anti-Patterns to Avoid
docs.text: Anti-Pattern Problem Fix Megazord State One state handles everything Split into single-responsibility states Dead End Error state with no transitions out Add recovery/retry transitions Infinite Loop State transitions back to itself Add max retry logic or a fallback transition Context Blackhole Too many required_context_keys at once Collect progressively across states

docs.title: Testing FSMs
docs.text:
# Validate structure
from fsm_llm import validate_fsm_from_file
result = validate_fsm_from_file("my_fsm.json")  # checks reachability, missing transitions

Or from the command line:

fsm-llm-validate --fsm my_fsm.json

Test all paths, context flow, and edge cases (empty input, very long input, off-topic).

Next: Handler Development

docs.title: Handler Development Guide
docs.text:
Covers FSM-LLM v0.13.0

Handlers extend FSM behavior with custom logic at 8 lifecycle points. They can validate data, call external APIs, log interactions, implement business rules, and trigger side effects.

docs.title: Basic Structure
docs.text:
def my_handler(context: dict) -> dict:
    """Handlers receive context, return updates to merge back."""
    return {"new_key": "new_value"}

docs.title: Handler Timing Points
docs.text: The timings fire in the same order on a converse turn and on a message-free step (API.advance, and each step of API.run_until_terminal); a step only has no user message. run_until_terminal(..., before_step=fn) also calls fn(step_number) before each step, outside the turn: it may write context with api.update_context, and that step sees it.

docs.title: START_CONVERSATION -- Conversation begins
docs.text:
def welcome(context):
    user_id = context.get("user_id")
    return {"preferences": load_prefs(user_id)} if user_id else {}

api.register_handler(
    api.create_handler("Welcome").at(HandlerTiming.START_CONVERSATION).do(welcome))

docs.title: PRE_PROCESSING -- Before LLM processes input
docs.text: Good for input sanitization, PII detection, pre-validation.

docs.title: POST_PROCESSING -- After Pass 1 (extraction + transition), before Pass 2 (response)
docs.text: Good for entity extraction, context enrichment, analytics. Note: the transition has already fired, so .on_state(X) here matches the destination state, not the state that performed the extraction. To react to a specific state's extraction, use CONTEXT_UPDATE.on_state(X).

docs.title: CONTEXT_UPDATE -- When specific context keys change
docs.text:
api.register_handler(
    api.create_handler("EmailValidator")
        .on_context_update("email")  # shorthand for .at(CONTEXT_UPDATE).when_keys_updated("email")
        .do(validate_email))

docs.title: PRE_TRANSITION / POST_TRANSITION -- Before/after state change
docs.text:
api.register_handler(
    api.create_handler("OnCheckout")
        .on_state_entry("checkout")  # shorthand for .at(POST_TRANSITION).on_target_state("checkout")
        .do(check_inventory))

docs.title: END_CONVERSATION -- Conversation ends
docs.text: Good for resource cleanup, saving summaries, releasing locks.

docs.title: ERROR -- On an exception while processing a message
docs.text:
Good for graceful recovery, fallback responses, error logging.

ERROR handlers fire on any FSMError (including LLMResponseError, the LLM-outage case) raised while converse or converse_stream processes a message; the FSMError is still re-raised to the caller. They do not fire for a failure inside start_conversation (for example the LLM being down during the greeting). The handler context carries the usual keys plus _error (the message) and _traceback. They run after the turn has been rolled back, so:

  • The dict an ERROR handler returns is not merged into the conversation (it is dropped and debug-logged). Use api.update_context(conversation_id, {...}) to write context from an ERROR handler.
  • Re-entering the same conversation raises. Calling converse or converse_stream on the conversation whose turn is in flight (from any handler timing, or between next() calls of an open stream) raises FSMError ("already being processed") instead of nesting. update_context and the read methods stay allowed.
  • KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit and GeneratorExit run no handlers.

docs.title: HandlerBuilder Reference
docs.text:
The fluent API returned by api.create_handler(name):

Method Description .at(*timings) Specify one or more HandlerTiming values .on_state(*states) Execute only in these states .not_on_state(*states) Exclude these states .on_target_state(*states) Execute only when transitioning TO these states .not_on_target_state(*states) Exclude transitions TO these states .when_context_has(*keys) Require these context keys to exist .when_keys_updated(*keys) Execute when these keys change .on_state_entry(*states) Shorthand: .at(POST_TRANSITION).on_target_state() .on_state_exit(*states) Shorthand: .at(PRE_TRANSITION).on_state() .on_context_update(*keys) Shorthand: .at(CONTEXT_UPDATE).when_keys_updated(*keys) .when(condition) Custom lambda: (timing, state, target, ctx, keys) -> bool .with_priority(n) Execution priority (lower runs first, default 100) .critical(value=True) Mark the handler critical -- failures always raise (see Error Handling) .do(fn) Set handler function and build

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
The HandlerSystem takes a handler_error_mode, a HandlerErrorMode (importable from fsm_llm) or its string value. API, FSMManager and the builders' set_handler_error_mode take the same value under the same name, and an unknown value raises ValueError naming handler_error_mode: - HandlerErrorMode.CONTINUE / "continue" (default) -- Log error, skip failed handler, continue with others - HandlerErrorMode.RAISE / "raise" -- Stop execution, propagate exception

When no handler subscribes to a timing, the pipeline skips that timing entirely (no context deep-copy, no call), so an FSM without handlers pays nothing for the hook points. The subscription check (HandlerSystem.handlers_at) is an optional fast-path hook: a duck-typed handler_system that only implements execute_handlers still works, it just skips the shortcut.

Handlers marked critical=True always raise regardless of error mode. There are two ways to mark one -- a BaseHandler subclass, or .critical() on the fluent builder:

# Fluent builder
api.create_handler("audit").at(HandlerTiming.POST_TRANSITION).critical().do(write_audit_record)

class PaymentHandler(BaseHandler):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(name="PaymentHandler", critical=True)

    def should_execute(self, timing, current_state, target_state, context, updated_keys):
        return timing == HandlerTiming.POST_TRANSITION and current_state == "process_payment"

    def execute(self, context):
        return process_payment(context)  # failure always propagates

docs.title: External API Calls
docs.text:
Handlers execute synchronously. Use requests or concurrent.futures for I/O:

def check_inventory(context):
    product_id = context.get("selected_product_id")
    if not product_id:
        return {}
    try:
        resp = requests.get(f"https://api.store.com/inventory/{product_id}", timeout=10)
        if resp.ok:
            data = resp.json()
            return {"in_stock": data["quantity"] > 0, "quantity": data["quantity"]}
    except requests.RequestException:
        pass
    return {"inventory_check_failed": True}

api.register_handler(
    api.create_handler("Inventory").on_state_entry("product_selection").do(check_inventory))

docs.title: Conditional Execution
docs.text:
api.register_handler(
    api.create_handler("PremiumBenefits")
        .at(HandlerTiming.POST_TRANSITION)
        .when(lambda t, s, tgt, ctx, keys: ctx.get("user_tier") == "premium")
        .do(lambda ctx: {"discount_rate": 0.20, "free_shipping": True}))

docs.title: Validation Chain
docs.text:
api.register_handler(
    api.create_handler("AgeValidator")
        .on_context_update("age")
        .with_priority(10)
        .do(validate_age))

api.register_handler(
    api.create_handler("ConsentValidator")
        .on_context_update("age_group", "parental_consent")
        .with_priority(20)
        .do(validate_consent))

docs.title: Exclusion Filters
docs.text:
# Run on every state EXCEPT "error" and "done"
api.register_handler(
    api.create_handler("GlobalLogger")
        .at(HandlerTiming.POST_PROCESSING)
        .not_on_state("error", "done")
        .do(lambda ctx: {"logged": True}))

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Keep handlers focused -- One handler, one responsibility
  2. Handle errors gracefully -- Always expect failures in external calls
  3. Choose the right timing -- Use the most specific timing point
  4. Use priority for ordering -- Lower numbers run first
  5. Avoid side effects in validators -- Pure validation, no database writes
  6. Test handlers in isolation -- They're just functions that take and return dicts

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
def test_email_validator():
    assert validate_email({"email": "user@example.com"})["email_valid"] is True
    assert validate_email({"email": "invalid"})["email_valid"] is False
    assert validate_email({})["email_valid"] is False

def test_handler_execution_order():
    order = []
    api.register_handler(api.create_handler("H1").at(HandlerTiming.PRE_PROCESSING)
        .with_priority(10).do(lambda ctx: order.append("H1") or {}))
    api.register_handler(api.create_handler("H2").at(HandlerTiming.PRE_PROCESSING)
        .with_priority(20).do(lambda ctx: order.append("H2") or {}))
    conv_id, _ = api.start_conversation()
    api.converse("test", conv_id)
    assert order == ["H1", "H2"]

docs.title: Handlers in Extension Packages
docs.text:
• Agents: POST_TRANSITION executes tools, PRE_TRANSITION enforces budgets, CONTEXT_UPDATE checks HITL approval
  • Reasoning: Validation, tracing, context pruning, retry limiting handlers
  • Monitor: Registers at all 8 timing points (priority 9999) as pure observers -- returns {}, never modifies state
  • Workflows: Manages step execution directly via async pipeline; ConversationStep has its own handler system

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Testing shows how to test a handler with a scripted model.
  • The API Reference lists HandlerBuilder, HandlerTiming and HandlerErrorMode.
  • Architecture shows where the eight points sit in a turn.

docs.title: Quick Start Tutorial
docs.text:
Covers FSM-LLM v0.13.0

Welcome to FSM-LLM! This tutorial will have you building stateful conversations with LLMs in minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or higher
  • An LLM: a local Ollama model (name it with LLM_MODEL=ollama_chat/<tag>; there is no built-in default model), or any LiteLLM provider such as OpenAI with its API key (set LLM_MODEL and the provider's key)

docs.title: 1. Installation
docs.text:
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install llm-fsm

# With extensions
pip install "llm-fsm[monitor]"      # Real-time monitoring dashboard (fastapi, uvicorn, jinja2)
pip install "llm-fsm[all]"          # Every optional dependency

The distribution is llm-fsm; the import package is fsm_llm. fsm-llm on PyPI is a different, unrelated project: if you installed it by mistake, run pip uninstall fsm-llm first. The reasoning, workflows, agents, eval and synthesis extras add no packages (that code ships in every install); extras only add third-party dependencies.

Classification is built into the core package -- no extra install needed.

docs.title: 2. Set Your API Key
docs.text:
export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-api-key-here"
# Or create a .env file and load it on purpose (nothing reads it unasked):
echo "OPENAI_API_KEY=your-api-key-here" > .env
# Python: fsm_llm.load_env()      CLI: fsm-llm --env-file .env --fsm your_fsm.json

Environment variables used by the library and the fsm-llm command:

Variable Default Meaning LLM_MODEL none litellm model id. Required by the fsm-llm CLI; the API class uses it when no model= is passed, and raises ModelNotConfiguredError when neither is set LLM_TEMPERATURE 0.5 CLI only LLM_MAX_TOKENS 1000 CLI only FSM_PATH none not usable with fsm-llm: --fsm is checked first and is mandatory OPENAI_API_KEY etc. none provider keys, read by litellm

Importing fsm_llm loads no .env file. Call fsm_llm.load_env() (it searches from the working directory upward, or takes a path, and does not replace a variable the process already has, except a blank one, which counts as unset; to keep a variable empty on purpose, do not name it in the file) or pass --env-file PATH to fsm-llm, fsm-llm-eval, fsm-llm-meta, python -m fsm_llm.reasoning or fsm-llm-monitor; otherwise export the variables.

docs.title: 3. Your First Bot
docs.text:
Create hello_bot.py:

from fsm_llm import API

greeting_fsm = {
    "name": "friendly_greeter",
    "description": "Greets the user, learns their name, then says goodbye",
    "initial_state": "welcome",
    "states": {
        "welcome": {
            "id": "welcome",
            "description": "Greet the user and collect their name",
            "purpose": "Greet the user warmly and ask for their name",
            "extraction_instructions": "Extract the user's name.",
            "response_instructions": "Warmly greet the user and ask for their name.",
            "required_context_keys": ["name"],
            "transitions": [{
                "target_state": "personalized",
                "description": "Once the user has given their name",
                "conditions": [{
                    "description": "The name has been extracted",
                    "requires_context_keys": ["name"],
                    "logic": {"has_context": "name"}
                }]
            }]
        },
        "personalized": {
            "id": "personalized",
            "description": "Talk to the user by name",
            "purpose": "Give a personalized response using their name",
            "extraction_instructions": "Extract how the user says they are doing, as mood_reply.",
            "response_instructions": "Use their name and ask how they're doing.",
            "transitions": [{
                "target_state": "farewell",
                "description": "After user responds about their day"
            }]
        },
        "farewell": {
            "id": "farewell",
            "description": "Say goodbye",
            "purpose": "Wish them well and say goodbye",
            "response_instructions": "Wish them well using their name and say goodbye.",
            "transitions": []
        }
    }
}

api = API.from_definition(greeting_fsm, model="gpt-4o-mini")
conv_id, response = api.start_conversation()
print(f"Bot: {response}")

while not api.has_conversation_ended(conv_id):
    user_input = input("You: ")
    response = api.converse(user_input, conv_id)
    print(f"Bot: {response}")

print(f"\nCollected data: {api.get_data(conv_id)}")

Run it: python hello_bot.py

Gating: required_context_keys only tells the pipeline which keys to extract in a state; it never blocks a transition. The welcome -> personalized move is held back by the transition condition (requires_context_keys plus a has_context rule), so the bot keeps asking until a name has been extracted. A transition with no conditions fires on the first message.

docs.title: 4. Add a Handler
docs.text:
Handlers add custom logic at 8 lifecycle points:

from fsm_llm import API, HandlerTiming

api = API.from_definition(greeting_fsm, model="gpt-4o-mini")

def detect_mood(context):
    # Handlers see the context DATA (extracted keys plus a few "_" keys such as
    # _conversation_id), not the raw user message: read an extracted key.
    response = str(context.get("mood_reply", "")).lower()
    positive = ["good", "great", "wonderful", "amazing"]
    negative = ["bad", "terrible", "awful", "stressed"]
    if any(w in response for w in positive):
        return {"mood": "positive"}
    elif any(w in response for w in negative):
        return {"mood": "negative", "offer_help": True}
    return {"mood": "neutral"}

api.register_handler(
    api.create_handler("MoodDetector")
        .at(HandlerTiming.CONTEXT_UPDATE)
        .on_state("personalized")
        .do(detect_mood)
)

Timing note: use CONTEXT_UPDATE to react to what was extracted in a state -- it fires after that state's extraction with current_state still set to it. POST_PROCESSING runs after the transition, so .on_state(X) there matches the destination state, not the state that did the extracting.

docs.title: 5. Streaming and Persistence
docs.text:
Stream the response tokens as they are generated, instead of waiting for the full reply:

for chunk in api.converse_stream(user_input, conv_id):
    print(chunk, end="", flush=True)

Persist conversations across process restarts by attaching a session store:

from fsm_llm import API, FileSessionStore

store = FileSessionStore("./sessions")
api = API.from_definition(greeting_fsm, model="gpt-4o-mini", session_store=store)
conv_id, response = api.start_conversation()
# State auto-saves after each converse() call. To resume later (e.g. a new process):
new_conv_id, state = api.restore_session(conv_id)

docs.title: 6. More Ways to Build
docs.text: The conversation above is one way in. The rest of the library is built from the same parts, and the sections below show a builder, an agent, a workflow and the reasoning engine in a few lines each. greeter.json in the builder example stands for any FSM definition file, for example your own saved copy of the friendly_greeter dictionary above or the greeter.json of the project README.

docs.title: Assemble It Step by Step
docs.text:
Anything with more than a couple of settings can be put together by chaining calls. While you chain, nothing is checked; the final .build() checks everything at once and hands back a private copy, so one recipe can make many independent objects.

A conversation with a hook and a model:

from fsm_llm import APIBuilder, HandlerTiming, create_handler

audit = (
    create_handler("audit")
    .at(HandlerTiming.POST_TRANSITION)
    .do(lambda context: {"audited": True})
)

api = (
    APIBuilder()
    .set_definition("greeter.json")
    .set_model("ollama_chat/qwen3.5:4b")
    .set_temperature(0.2)
    .add_handler(audit)
    .build()
)

An agent with a tool, an instruction and an iteration limit (a real run against the local model; the wording differs each time):

from fsm_llm.agents import ConfiguredAgentBuilder, tool


@tool
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two integers."""
    return a + b


agent = (
    ConfiguredAgentBuilder()
    .set_pattern("react")
    .add_tool(add)
    .set_system_prompt("Answer in one short sentence.")
    .set_max_iterations(6)
    .build()
)
result = agent("What is 19 + 23? Use the add tool.")
print(result.answer, result.success, result.stop_reason)
# 19 + 23 equals 42, as calculated by the add tool. True answered

Mistakes come back together, in one error, instead of one at a time:

from fsm_llm import APIBuilder, BuildError

try:
    APIBuilder().set_llm_option("model", "a").set_llm_option("max_history_size", 3).build()
except BuildError as err:
    print(*err.errors, sep="\n")
# option 'model' names a constructor parameter; use set_model()
# option 'max_history_size' names a constructor parameter; use set_max_history_size()

What you get from this style:

  • Setters only record, so you can chain them in any order and pass the half-built recipe around.
  • One .build() does all the checking and raises one error type. BuildError is a ValueError that lists every problem in .errors and keeps the underlying cause attached.
  • The result is a private copy: change the recipe afterwards, or build again, and nothing already built moves. Objects you hand in (a model interface, a tool, a store) stay shared, not copied.
  • Settings that pass straight through to the model library are accepted without a whitelist, and a name that clashes with a typed setter is refused with a message that names the setter to use.
  • It is an alternative, not a replacement: the plain constructors and from_file still work everywhere.

The same shape builds conversations, agents of any pattern, workflows, agent graphs and handlers. The rules are in API Reference.

docs.title: Create an Agent in One Line
docs.text:
from fsm_llm.agents import AgentConfig, create_agent, tool


@tool
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two integers."""
    return a + b


agent = create_agent("react", [add], config=AgentConfig(model="ollama_chat/qwen3.5:4b"))   # or set LLM_MODEL
result = agent("What is 19 + 23? Use the add tool.")
print(result.answer, result.success, result.stop_reason)   # 19 + 23 equals 42. True answered

success is True only when the run reached its goal. A forced stop still returns its last answer, with success=False and a stop_reason.

docs.title: Run a Workflow (No LLM Needed)
docs.text:
This prints WorkflowStatus.COMPLETED:

import asyncio
from fsm_llm.workflows import WorkflowEngine, auto_step, condition_step, create_workflow_builder

wf = (
    create_workflow_builder("orders", "Order check")
    .set_initial_step(auto_step("load", "Load order", next_step_id="route",
                                action=lambda ctx: {"amount": 1500}))
    .add_step(condition_step("route", "Big order?", condition=lambda ctx: ctx["amount"] >= 1000,
                             true_step_id="review", false_step_id="done"))
    .add_step(auto_step("review", "Manual review", next_step_id="done"))
    .add_step(auto_step("done", "Finish", next_step_id=""))
    .build()
)


async def main():
    engine = WorkflowEngine()
    engine.register_workflow(wf)
    instance_id = await engine.start("orders")
    print(engine.get_status(instance_id))


asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Solve a Problem with the Reasoning Engine
docs.text:
from fsm_llm.reasoning import ReasoningEngine

engine = ReasoningEngine(model="ollama_chat/qwen3.5:4b")
solution, trace = engine.solve_problem("If all cats are mammals and Tom is a cat, what is Tom?")
print(solution)
print(trace["summary"])

python examples/intermediate/book_recommendation/run.py  # Multi-branch conversations

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
1. States -- Each conversation step with a single purpose
  2. Transitions -- Rules for moving between states (JsonLogic conditions)
  3. Context -- Data collected and remembered across turns
  4. Handlers -- Custom logic at 8 lifecycle points
  5. FSM Stacking -- Nested sub-conversations via push_fsm/pop_fsm

docs.title: Useful Commands
docs.text:
fsm-llm --fsm your_fsm.json           # Run any FSM interactively (needs LLM_MODEL, --model or --env-file)
fsm-llm-validate --fsm your_fsm.json  # Validate FSM structure
fsm-llm-visualize --fsm your_fsm.json # ASCII visualization
fsm-llm-monitor                       # Launch monitoring dashboard

docs.title: Common Patterns
docs.text:
Information gathering -- Use required_context_keys to have the data extracted, and a transition condition (requires_context_keys + has_context) to stay in the state until it is collected.

Branching logic -- Multiple transitions with conditions route to different states.

Error handling -- Register a handler at HandlerTiming.ERROR for graceful recovery.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Issue Solution "No API key found" echo $OPENAI_API_KEY -- ensure it's set "State not found" Run fsm-llm-validate --fsm your_fsm.json "Context key missing" Add a debug handler at POST_PROCESSING to print context keys

docs.title: Reporting Vulnerabilities
docs.text: Report security vulnerabilities to nikolasmarkou@gmail.com.

docs.title: Supply Chain Security
docs.text:
• pyproject.toml bounds every dependency it declares (the core dependencies, every extra, the docs group and the build backend) on both sides, and no declared range admits a major version other than the tested one: the first version component of every floor equals that of the exact pin in constraints.txt, and the ceiling is the next major (the major of a 0.x pin is 0, so those ranges are bounded by <1). The one named exception is the build backend setuptools>=77,<85 (the same range is in the dev extra): setuptools has no stable major semantics, so its floor is the first release that supports what the project needs (77, the PEP 639 license expression) and its ceiling is the release after the pinned 84, which keeps an sdist build from picking an untested setuptools. tests/test_packaging.py::TestNoRangeAdmitsAnUntestedMajor fails on any other range, and TestDeclaredRangesMatchPins on one with no upper bound or without its pin; the release build runs under the pins of constraints.txt.
  • The compromised litellm releases 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 are excluded by the litellm>=1.109.0 floor. No != specifiers are used.
  • CI runs .pth file auditing on every build (scripts/audit_pth.py, in the lint job and on every leg of the test matrix)
  • CI audits the installed environment, transitive dependencies included, with pip-audit --skip-editable in the job supply-chain on every push and pull request, and a known vulnerability in any installed package fails the build. A canary step in the same job runs pip-audit over tests/fixtures/canary-vulnerable-pins.txt (pins of old releases with published advisories, never installed) and passes only when the audit exits 1 with a non-empty report, so a broken audit, a changed exit code or an unreachable advisory source turns the build red instead of passing silently. pip-audit is pinned in constraints.txt and listed in the dev extra.
  • Every GitHub Action in .github/workflows is pinned to a full commit SHA with its release tag in a trailing comment, and a checkout keeps no credentials except in the two jobs that push (the docs deploy and the pin refresh propose). tests/test_fsm_llm_regression/test_supply_chain.py reads every workflow file and fails on a floating tag, on pull_request_target, on a workflow with no read-only top-level token and on a write scope outside its allowlist. The allowlist today is six grants on five jobs: contents: write on the docs deploy job (it pushes the site on a version tag), pull-requests: write on the dependency-review job (its failure comment), contents: write plus pull-requests: write on the propose job of refresh-pins.yml (it pushes a branch and opens a pull request), id-token: write on the publish job of release.yml (the OIDC token that PyPI trusted publishing exchanges for a short-lived upload token) and contents: write on its github-release job (it creates the GitHub release of the pushed tag). A second rule keeps third-party code away from those tokens: no job that holds a write scope installs a package or runs project code (an installer, an interpreter, a test runner, a project script or a setup-* action in such a job fails the same test). There is one named waiver, the docs deploy job: it installs the docs tools to run mike, and they are pinned exactly in constraints.txt, are never moved by the weekly pin refresh (which changes litellm and mcp only) and change only in a reviewed commit, so no new third-party release reaches that job unreviewed; the waiver and its reason are pinned in the test.
  • A scheduled workflow, .github/workflows/refresh-pins.yml (weekly and on demand), proposes newer litellm and mcp pins through scripts/refresh_pins.py. A release is eligible only after a 7-day cooldown (the litellm 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 releases were malware for hours, and a bad release is usually yanked within days), and only when it is stable, not yanked, admits every Python of the test matrix and stays in the major of the current pin; the script never downgrades and never crosses a major. When a pin moves, the test job installs it and runs the whole non-slow suite, mypy, the .pth audit and pip-audit, and only after it passed does the propose job push a branch and open a pull request (a pull request opened with the default token does not trigger the CI workflow, so the gate runs in the workflow itself). The split is the point: the test job executes a brand-new third-party release, so it has the read-only token and no credentials, and it uploads the three files of the proposal (constraints.txt, pyproject.toml and the script's report) as an artifact before it installs anything; the propose job holds the write token, installs nothing and runs no project code, and a guard step refuses anything but those three regular files and any change beyond the litellm and mcp pin and range lines. The pull request is reviewed and merged by the owner; nothing is merged automatically.
  • Releases are made by one workflow, .github/workflows/release.yml, which starts on a pushed tag v* and on nothing else. The package is built once (sdist and wheel, with the build backend under the pins of constraints.txt), checked with twine check --strict, the tag against src/fsm_llm/__version__.py (final releases only) and the release notes against CHANGELOG.md, and the same files are then uploaded to PyPI by trusted publishing: the publish job holds the only id-token: write, runs in the GitHub environment pypi (a required reviewer must approve the deployment), is a plain hosted job with no container and no reusable workflow, and publishes PEP 740 attestations with the files. There is no long-lived PyPI credential anywhere (no API token, no password, no secret), and twine upload is never used: the workflow tests fail on either. The workflow also writes an SBOM (CycloneDX 1.6 JSON, cyclonedx-py environment over a fresh environment with the wheel installed with every extra; cyclonedx-bom is pinned in constraints.txt) and attaches it, with the distributions and the notes, to the GitHub release; the SBOM is not attested and is not on PyPI.
  • Dependency review (actions/dependency-review-action) runs on pull requests and fails a pull request that adds a dependency with a high or critical advisory.
  • The workflows are linted with actionlint and zizmor in the lint job; both are pinned in constraints.txt, and zizmor runs offline (its online audits need a token that the lint job does not name).
  • constraints.txt pins every direct dependency and the build backend to one exact version for dev/CI reproducibility (for example litellm==1.109.1)

docs.text: litellm versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 contained credential-stealing malware injected via .pth file. See CHANGELOG.md for details and remediation steps.

docs.title: Runtime FSM Synthesis
docs.text:
Covers FSM-LLM v0.13.0

Some conversations cannot be written ahead of time. "Collect what this visa form needs" depends on a goal that only shows up at run time. fsm_llm.synthesis lets a host conversation ask for a procedure by goal: a model writes a finite state machine (FSM) for it, a stack of checks decides whether that FSM may run, a library stores it, and a runner executes it as a child of the host conversation.

Status of the evidence. The code is tested offline with scripted models. The pre-registered live comparison, scripts/synthesis_bench.py (compiled FSM against an in-context ReAct agent, with a hand-written FSM as a harness check), ran three blocks, s0, s1 and s2, and every verdict is INCONCLUSIVE. Every role and every arm used the same model, ollama_chat/bonsai-2:27b (Q2_0, 2-bit): there is NO strong/cheap split, so no strong-compile/cheap-run cost asymmetry was tested. No result in these docs says a compiled procedure helps; see "Live results" below.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Use it when the shape of a sub-conversation is known only at run time and you want the host's own, usually cheaper, model to run it with guardrails. Do not use it when you can write the FSM yourself: a hand-written FSM is cheaper, easier to review and is what the bench will compare against. A procedure cannot call tools (the runner refuses a completion state), cannot set a persona and cannot be longer than the policy allows (12 states by default).

import fsm_llm loads no synthesis code. Import it by name:

from fsm_llm.synthesis import FSMLibrary, FSMSynthesizer, ProcedureRunner

The synthesis extra adds no dependency, there is no console script, and importing fsm_llm.synthesis also imports fsm_llm.agents (and through it fsm_llm.reasoning) and fsm_llm.eval. Nothing in core imports it back.

docs.title: The concierge pattern
docs.text:
A host FSM names a procedure with a synthesize state. The state is silent (no response_instructions), carries the goal and the key names, and routes on synthesis_result.status. Save this as concierge.json:

{
  "name": "Concierge",
  "description": "Greets a guest and books a table with a procedure written on demand",
  "initial_state": "greet",
  "persona": "A calm, friendly concierge",
  "states": {
    "greet": {
      "id": "greet",
      "description": "Welcome the guest",
      "purpose": "Greet the guest",
      "response_instructions": "Welcome the guest to the venue.",
      "transitions": [{"target_state": "gather", "description": "Always continue"}]
    },
    "gather": {
      "id": "gather",
      "description": "Run the booking procedure",
      "purpose": "Collect the party size and the date",
      "response_instructions": "",
      "synthesize": {
        "goal": "Book a table: ask the party size and the date.",
        "inputs": ["venue"],
        "return_keys": ["party_size", "visit_date"],
        "on_failure": "sorry"
      },
      "transitions": [
        {
          "target_state": "done",
          "description": "The procedure returned the booking",
          "priority": 1,
          "conditions": [{
            "description": "The procedure finished",
            "requires_context_keys": ["synthesis_result"],
            "logic": {"==": [{"var": "synthesis_result.status"}, "ok"]}
          }]
        },
        {
          "target_state": "sorry",
          "description": "The procedure failed or was stopped",
          "priority": 2,
          "conditions": [{
            "description": "The procedure did not finish",
            "requires_context_keys": ["synthesis_result"],
            "logic": {"in": [{"var": "synthesis_result.status"}, ["failed", "aborted"]]}
          }]
        }
      ]
    },
    "done": {
      "id": "done",
      "description": "Booking confirmed",
      "purpose": "Confirm the booking",
      "response_instructions": "Confirm the booking using party_size and visit_date."
    },
    "sorry": {
      "id": "sorry",
      "description": "Booking failed",
      "purpose": "Apologise",
      "response_instructions": "Apologise and say the booking could not be made."
    }
  }
}

The loader checks a synthesize state against the real transition evaluator, so a wrong edge fails at load, not in production:

  • Every edge of the state must read synthesis_result (or a handler_only_keys entry), or it would fire before the runner has produced a result.
  • No edge may pass while the result is absent or running.
  • The edge to on_failure must pass for status failed AND for aborted. Write it as status in [failed, aborted]. A bare == "failed" is refused, because an aborted procedure would otherwise strand the host.
  • A synthesize state declares no extraction and no completion, and on_failure must be one of its own transition targets.

The runner drives the host. This runs offline with scripted interfaces (Strong stands in for the strong model, Host for the host's cheap model); with real models you pass FSMSynthesizer(model="...") and an API built the usual way:

import json
import tempfile

from fsm_llm import API
from fsm_llm.core.definitions import (
    CompletionResponse,
    FieldExtractionResponse,
    ResponseGenerationResponse,
)
from fsm_llm.llm import LLMInterface
from fsm_llm.synthesis import FSMLibrary, FSMSynthesizer, ProcedureRunner
from fsm_llm.synthesis.prompts import EXAMPLE_FSM

with open("concierge.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    host = json.load(f)


class Strong(LLMInterface):  # the compiler: returns a ready FSM as JSON text
    calls = 0

    def complete(self, request):
        self.calls += 1
        return CompletionResponse(kind="final", text=json.dumps(EXAMPLE_FSM))

    def generate_response(self, request):
        raise NotImplementedError


class Host(LLMInterface):  # the cheap model that runs the host and the child
    answers = {"party_size": 4, "visit_date": "Friday"}

    def generate_response(self, request):
        return ResponseGenerationResponse(message="ok", message_type="response", reasoning="")

    def extract_field(self, request):
        value = self.answers.get(request.field_name)
        return FieldExtractionResponse(
            field_name=request.field_name, value=value, is_valid=value is not None,
            confidence=1.0 if value is not None else 0.0, reasoning="",
        )

    def complete(self, request):
        raise NotImplementedError


strong = Strong()
api = API.from_definition(host, llm_interface=Host())
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as root:
    synth = FSMSynthesizer(strong, library=FSMLibrary(root))
    runner = ProcedureRunner(api, host, synth)
    for _ in range(2):
        conv_id, _ = api.start_conversation({"venue": "Luna"})
        runner.run(conv_id, max_steps=40)          # message-free; or runner.converse(conv_id, "four, Friday")
        print(api.get_current_state(conv_id), api.get_data(conv_id)["synthesis_result"]["status"])
    print(strong.calls)                            # 1: the second booking reused the stored procedure

The output is done ok twice, then 1. Drive the host through the runner (run, converse, end_conversation), not through API alone: a bare API.converse on a synthesize state finds no extraction and no passing edge, so it stays in the state. The runner is the thing that gives the field its meaning.

docs.title: The synthesizer
docs.text:
FSMSynthesizer(llm=None, *, model=None, policy=None, library=None, reviewer=None, embed=None, simulator=None) takes exactly one of llm (anything implementing complete) or model (it builds a LiteLLMInterface). Two methods matter:

  • compile(goal, *, inputs=(), return_keys) -> CompileResult asks the strong model for FSM JSON, runs the gates and, when they fail, sends the failures back as text for up to policy.max_repair_rounds more rounds. It raises SynthesisError when no round passes. A provider outage raises it too, chained from LLMResponseError, with no retry. A reply cut at max_tokens is a failed round and is never parsed.
  • obtain(goal, *, inputs=(), return_keys, min_lifecycle="verified") -> Procedure searches the library first and compiles on a miss. Procedure.source is library or compiled.

docs.title: The gates
docs.text:
Every compile runs these checks, in this order, and reports all failures, not just the first:

  1. G1, loads. The JSON loads as a core FSMDefinition, exactly as API would load it.
  2. G2, structure. The core FSMValidator reports no error. Its warnings never fail a compile, and G2 is never stricter than the loader.
  3. G3, data flow (fsm_llm.core.verify.flow). A key an edge reads must be extracted earlier on every path, or be a declared input. Each return key must be guaranteed when the procedure ends.
  4. G4, liveness (fsm_llm.core.verify.flow). No trap, no loop without an exit that can fire, no edge hidden behind an unconditional edge of lower priority number, no permanent tie, no path longer than policy.max_turns.
  5. G5, policy (policy.check_policy). Limits on states, edges, fields and text; reserved names; no persona; no secret-looking or internal key names; no model setting on a classification entry; no regular expression in a validation rule; completion tools only from policy.allowed_tools; no synthesize state inside a procedure unless max_synthesis_depth is above 1 (the default is 1). It is an allow-list of fields, so a field nobody thought of is refused.
  6. G6a, dead edges (dryrun.py). It tries a small pool of values per key through the real evaluator and reports an edge no assignment can fire. No model call. It is coarse on purpose: anything outside the fragment it understands counts as possibly firing, so it never rejects a good procedure for what it cannot read.
  7. G6b, simulation (simulation.py), only when a Simulator is given. A scripted happy path built from the definition, plus scenarios of four kinds written by one model call (missing_info, correction, off_topic, adversarial), are played against the procedure on the simulator's interface. It passes when the happy path and the overall pass rate both reach policy.min_pass_rate (default 0.5) and the happy path moves past the first state. require_simulation=True makes it mandatory.
  8. G7, approval. Required when policy.require_approval is set or a completion state lists tools. See Approval below.

When the gates pass, an abort path is injected: a silent abort terminal state and a priority 0 edge to it from every non-terminal state, gated on the handler-only key procedure_abort. The runner sets that key when the child spends its turn budget, so no model reply can forge or block it. G1 and G2 run again on the injected form. The names abort, procedure_abort and synthesis_result are reserved: a compile may not declare, read or write them.

docs.title: What verified means
docs.text: A compiled procedure is stored as verified. That means the gates above passed: static checks, a dead-edge check and, if you passed a simulator, a bounded simulation over scenarios that a model wrote. It does not mean the procedure is correct. If the simulator runs on the same model that wrote the procedure, a passing simulation is partly the model agreeing with itself, which is a weaker signal than a separate judge. Review what matters before you trust it (see Approval).

docs.title: The library
docs.text:
FSMLibrary(path) is a directory. Each procedure is stored under the sha256 of its canonical definition: definitions/<sha256>.json and records/<sha256>.json, with traces/, scenarios/ and patches/ beside them. Every write goes to a temp file, is synced, then replaced into place; a corrupt file raises LibraryError and is never overwritten, and a symlink is refused. Two processes on one directory are last writer wins on the run counters.

A record has a lifecycle: draft, verified, trusted, deprecated. A compile is stored verified. A human moves it to trusted with library.approve(digest, by), or run counts do when policy.trust_after_successes is set (never for a repaired child). Nothing leaves deprecated. A synthesize state's min_lifecycle (verified or trusted) says which stored procedures it will run.

docs.title: Reuse
docs.text:
search first filters on the signature (every required input available, the return keys covered, the tools allowed, the lifecycle high enough), then scores the survivors against the stored goal:

  • With no embedder, only an identical goal reuses (lowercased, whitespace normalised; punctuation counts).
  • With an embedder (a function from a list of texts to vectors, embed=), the score is a cosine and a stored procedure is reused at or above policy.reuse_min_score (default 0.8). That is a similarity claim: cosine ignores negation, so "book a table" and "do not book a table" can match. For exact reuse, leave embed=None or set reuse_min_score=1.0.

A hit is re-verified (G1 to G6a on the stored form) before it runs. A hit that fails is skipped with a warning and a compile follows.

docs.title: Running a procedure
docs.text:
ProcedureRunner(api, definition, synthesizer, *, trace_sink=None) serves a host definition. Per conversation it settles three things as the host runs: it pops an ended child, aborts a child that spent policy.max_turns steps (it sets procedure_abort), and starts a pending synthesize state (write running, obtain, check that the procedure may run, push it as a child with no inherited context).

  • run(conversation_id, *, max_steps, max_seconds=None) runs message-free on core run_until_terminal. A spent budget raises RunBudgetExceededError.
  • converse(conversation_id, message) -> str is one user turn.
  • end_conversation(conversation_id) closes the conversation and drops the runner's bookkeeping; use it instead of API.end_conversation.

The child gets only the declared inputs and runs on the host's own interface. When it ends, only the declared return_keys come back, and only if every one is present and the child was not aborted. The result synthesis_result is {status, procedure_id, version, reason}: status is ok, failed, aborted or running, and reason is a fixed code or None, never exception text. The codes are inputs_missing, return_keys_missing, provider_error, library_error, compile_failed, push_failed, approval_required, approval_denied, reviewer_error, depth_refused, completion_unsupported, lifecycle_too_low, not_simulated, budget_spent and unexpected_error. Branch on the code, not on any message.

Things to know when you run one:

  • The result key is skip-if-set: a state that must run again on re-entry has to clear synthesis_result on entry (core clear_keys_on_entry). A child FSM you push yourself with API.push_fsm does not inherit the parent's value of its own synthesize result_key (the child's edges, which must read it, would route on the stale result before any run wrote one); pass it in context_to_pass if you want it.
  • One thread per conversation, like API.converse. The runner holds no lock.
  • A nested synthesize state (depth 2) works only for a procedure that returns one of its inputs.
  • policy.max_turns is the only turn bound. Core has none.
  • Two interfaces are metered separately: the strong one inside the synthesizer, the cheap one on the host API.

docs.title: Agent tools
docs.text:
create_procedure_tools(synthesizer, *, runner_llm, registry=None, max_obtains=20) -> ToolRegistry gives an agent two tools, for example ReactAgent(tools=registry):

  • obtain_procedure(goal, return_keys, inputs=[]) compiles or reuses and replies with a receipt: procedure_id, version, lifecycle, source, states, gates.
  • run_procedure(procedure_id, inputs={}) runs a stored procedure on runner_llm with no user messages and replies with its values, or failed: <code>. A procedure that needs a user answer replies failed: needs_user_input.

Both replies start with a fixed untrusted label, are capped and control-stripped, and carry codes, ids and defanged values only. The tool descriptions are module constants, never built from a goal or a record. Neither tool is flagged requires_approval: that flag makes four agent patterns refuse the registry, so approval happens inside the synthesizer instead. max_obtains caps compiles per registry, because a compile is the slow, costly call.

docs.title: Approval
docs.text:
A reviewer is a callable reviewer(request: ProcedureApprovalRequest) -> bool. It is asked on a compile only, never for a library hit, and it fails closed: a missing reviewer when approval is required, a reviewer that raises, and a result that is not exactly True all refuse the procedure, which is then not stored. request.text() shows a Mermaid diagram of the procedure, the gate verdicts, the goal and a size summary, and starts with a fixed untrusted label. reviewer_from_hitl(hitl) adapts a fsm_llm.agents.HumanInTheLoop.

from fsm_llm.synthesis import FSMSynthesizer, SynthesisPolicy

synth = FSMSynthesizer(
    strong,
    library=library,
    policy=SynthesisPolicy(require_approval=True),
    reviewer=lambda request: input(request.text() + "\nrun it? ") == "yes",
)

Approval records who approved (approved_by) as provenance. It does NOT make the record trusted: that needs library.approve(digest, by), a separate human edge.

docs.title: Traces, diagnosis and repair
docs.text:
Procedures that fail in use can be improved, and the loop is built so that a user cannot talk it into weakening a shared procedure.

  • Traces. TraceRecorder(library.add_trace) is a trace_sink for the runner. A RunTrace holds names, type names, state ids, counts and codes, never a value, user text or reply. library.read_traces(digest) returns (traces, skipped); a torn or hostile line is skipped and counted, and the file keeps the last 200 traces per procedure.
  • Diagnosis. diagnose(traces, definition, policy, *, return_keys=()) applies nine rules in a fixed order and returns Diagnosis objects with a code, the state, the keys and the share of runs. Only a run that failed for the procedure's own reasons (budget_spent, return_keys_missing) can justify a rewrite; an outage or a refusal is not-procedure-fault and is never patched.
  • Patch. propose_patch(diagnoses, definition, policy, llm) asks the model for RFC 6902 operations (add, remove, replace, test only), scoped to /states/<diagnosed state>/..., never the abort state, initial_state, persona or the handler-only list. apply_patch applies them to a copy and checks bounds before it walks anything.
  • Repair. repair_procedure(parent_digest, ops, *, library, synthesizer, simulator, replay_scripts=None, write=False) re-runs G1 to G6b on the patched child (and asks the approval reviewer again if the child now needs it), replays the parent's stored failing scenarios on parent and child, and returns a PromotionResult with the decision and the counts: promote, regressed or no-improvement, or a refusal code. By default it writes nothing. Only write=True with a promote verdict stores the child, as verified, never trusted, never with the parent's approver, and a trusted parent is never deprecated. Replay scripts come from the parent's stored scenarios plus the ones you pass; production traces are never used as scripts.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
SynthesisPolicy is a frozen dataclass; a bad value raises SynthesisError at construction and is never clamped. The defaults are in docs/api_reference.md (Synthesis). The ones to know:

  • Size of a procedure: max_states 12, max_transitions_per_state 6, max_fields_per_state 10, max_text_chars 600.
  • Compile: max_repair_rounds 3, max_compile_tokens 8192, max_synthesis_seconds 300.
  • Run: max_turns 40 steps of the child in total.
  • Simulation: max_sim_turns 12, sim_trials 2, min_pass_rate 0.5, max_simulation_calls 400.
  • Repair: repair_min_failures 3, max_repairs_per_lineage 3 (counted over the whole tree from the root).

docs.title: Live results
docs.text:
Three blocks of the comparison in scripts/synthesis_bench.py ran against ollama_chat/bonsai-2:27b on a local Ollama server (bench id synthesis; rows, summaries, reports and pre-registrations in scripts/bench_data/synthesis/). The compiler, scenario writer, executor, ReAct agent and hand-written arm are ONE model: there is no strong/cheap split, a G6b pass is partly the model agreeing with itself, and no cost saving from a cheaper runner could appear. 16 judge-free tasks in four families (collect, route, branch, retry), 3 trials each; the primary unit is the first trial of each task. The verdict rule (SUPPORTED needs S above R with Fisher p under 0.05) is byte-identical in all three blocks.

Block S first trial (Wilson 95%) H first trial R first trial All trials S / H / R of 48 pass^3 S / H / R S first-trial failures Verdict s0 6 of 16 (0.18 to 0.61) 8 of 16 14 of 16 27 / 26 / 40 6 / 8 / 12 10 (8 compile) INCONCLUSIVE (h = 8 of 16, below 10) s1 15 of 16 (0.72 to 0.99) 15 of 16 16 of 16 45 / 45 / 45 14 / 15 / 14 1 (compile) INCONCLUSIVE (ceiling: s = 15 and r = 16) s2 15 of 16 (0.72 to 0.99) 16 of 16 16 of 16 47 / 47 / 46 15 / 15 / 15 1 (compile) INCONCLUSIVE (ceiling: s = 15 and r = 16)

Cost per block (prompt plus completion tokens over all 144 rows, wall time of the arm):

Block S tokens S wall H tokens H wall R tokens R wall s0 826,182 + 186,111 5,433 s 183,186 + 27,663 945 s 536,759 + 92,680 2,869 s s1 616,130 + 133,987 3,923 s 175,211 + 26,435 869 s 536,759 + 93,411 2,848 s s2 613,642 + 130,506 3,991 s 157,326 + 23,863 822 s 536,759 + 92,601 2,902 s

How to read this:

  • No block shows a compiled procedure beating the ReAct agent. In s1 and s2 the three arms are within one task of each other on 16 tasks that this model has saturated, so the ceiling clause fires and the data cannot separate them. S is also the most expensive arm here: it pays a compile call and a bounded simulation (over 1,000 simulation calls per block), and with one model a reused procedure saves no cheaper-model cost. Reuse itself worked: 31 of 48 S rows in s1 and s2 made no compile call.
  • s0 to s1 to s2 are NOT independent tests. After each block the failures were read in the raw calls and fixed, and the next block ran on the same 16 tasks. The gain of S from 6 to 15 of 16 shows the diagnosed defects were real and fixed on those tasks; it does not show the approach generalises.
  • The hand-written arm and the ReAct arm are not comparable across blocks: the grader (s1) and two hand-written hints (s1, s2) changed between blocks, each disclosed in the pre-registration of the block that first used it.
  • Single trials of this model are noisy: S r2 passed trial 1 and failed trials 2 and 3 of s1 on the same stored procedure; the ReAct arm (r1, two trials) and the hand-written arm (y2, one trial) ran out of turns re-asking in s2.

What each round changed (generic changes under src/fsm_llm/synthesis/, no task text there; a hygiene test checks it):

  • s0 to s1 (D-091 to D-105): a compile-time instruction that names the key a gated state extracts; deterministic repair of a mismatched closing bracket in a compile reply; the loader's allowed JsonLogic operators in the compile prompt and in plain ASCII in the repair text; a note on what a key name is when a gate reads a computed one. Harness v2 (one grader for all arms, hand-written branch detail from the state's own question).
  • s1 to s2 (D-106, D-107): a compile prompt rule that a key the goal says to decide needs a value gate over the allowed values; the hand-written route hint says to pick the label that fits the need.
  • After s2 (D-108, D-109), NOT covered by any registered block: the compile prompt says missing is true only when a key is absent; a dead-edge repair line says the same once, and a failing happy-path repair line says that a key chosen from a list needs an in gate. They were checked by short smokes only (y2 passed without a repair; y3 passed after one round; S r4 failed twice before the second note existed; the smoke meant to check that second note was stopped at close before it ran a trial, so D-109 has no live check at all). No fourth block was run, so their effect is unmeasured.

Which rows predate which fix: every s0 row predates all of the above; s1 rows predate D-106 to D-109; s2 rows predate D-108 and D-109. The manifests of a block pin the source it ran against, so after later source edits report <block> refuses by design and the committed REPORT_<block>.txt is the record.

docs.title: Safety model
docs.text:
1. The goal is untrusted caller text. It reaches the strong model only inside a fenced block, cut to 2,000 characters, control characters stripped and the characters [ ] < > replaced, so it cannot spell a marker. It is never a setting or an instruction. System prompts are built from the policy alone.
  2. Model-written text never becomes a setting. G5 is an allow-list, and the persona, model, prompt settings and regular expressions of a compile are refused. Text from a compile, a receipt or an approval request reaches a model or a person under a fixed untrusted label.
  3. Return keys are the only way data leaves a child, and only on success. No goal, compile text, reply or provider text goes into an exception message, a finding, a result or a trace.
  4. The abort path hangs on a key no extraction can write.
  5. Repair needs positive evidence, a replay and, if asked, an approval; it is propose-only by default.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• The live comparison is inconclusive: three blocks, one model for every role and arm, 16 tasks the model has saturated, the later two in-sample after fixes made from earlier failures, and no fourth block. There is no measured claim that a compiled procedure beats a ReAct agent or saves anything; see "Live results".
  • Open defects seen live: a G6b false rejection when a label-restricted extraction instruction meets an edge with no value gate (the gate feeds the filler "sample"; D-106 and D-109 push the model toward an in gate, unmeasured); G6b passes some compiles that fail at run time; the 2-bit compiler repeats a dead edge when a repair line gives no reason; the ReAct and hand-written arms sometimes re-ask past max_iterations; G6a has an over-cap residual and the outage detection has blind spots (see above).
  • verified is not proof of correctness (see above). G6a is coarse and G6b is only as good as the scenarios a model wrote.
  • Procedures cannot call tools. A compile may list completion tools (and then needs approval), but the runner and run_procedure refuse to run one.
  • A corrupt library file blocks retrieval for the whole library until a human fixes it.
  • Two signals of misbehaviour (an out-of-scope intent and a raw malformed extraction) are not recorded by core, so diagnose cannot use them.
  • The runner marks a provider outage from the host interface's error counter (usage().errors). A host that calls reset_usage() during a run, or an interface with no meter, gets the outage recorded as budget_spent, which diagnose reads as a procedure fault. A shared interface can give a false outage mark, which fails closed.
  • Importing the package loads fsm_llm.agents, fsm_llm.reasoning and fsm_llm.eval.

See src/fsm_llm/synthesis/README.md and src/fsm_llm/synthesis/AGENTS.md for the file list and the contracts, and docs/api_reference.md for signatures.
